title: Isle of Man Lore
originalText: Manannán mac Lir: The island's legendary namesake and a Celtic sea god. He is said to protect the Isle of Man by shrouding it in his magical cloak—bringing down the mist to hide the land from approaching enemies. [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] Finn mac Cumhaill (Finn McCool): Irish mythology claims the island was formed when the giant Fionn scooped up a chunk of land to throw at a fleeing Scottish rival. He overshot, and the hunk of earth landed in the Irish Sea, creating the Isle of Man. The Moddey Dhoo (Black Dog): A ghostly black hound that is said to haunt the corridors of Peel Castle. According to local legend, a guard in a drunken stupor once defied the creature, resulting in his being stricken with terror and dying shortly after without being able to speak again. The Phynodderee : A hairy, giant goblin-like creature. Though incredibly strong and capable of doing a farmer's field work overnight, it can easily take offense and leave if it is gifted clothes, resulting in a lifelong grudge. The Buggane : A malevolent, shape-shifting goblin. The most famous tale involves a Buggane tearing the roof off St. Trinian's Church in a fit of rage. Hop Tu Naa: The Manx version of Halloween, celebrated on October 31st. Children traditionally carve turnips instead of pumpkins and sing traditional Hop Tu Naa songs, which are based around the legend of Jinny the Witch. Gef the Talking Mongoose: A famous 20th-century paranormal legend from Dalby. The Irving family claimed a small, intelligent, talking mongoose lived behind the wooden partition of their farmhouse, speaking, singing, and even hunting rabbits for them.

title: Philippines Lore
originalText: Aswang: A general term for shape-shifting evil entities that act as vampires, ghouls, or witches. Kapre: A tall, dark, hairy giant that sits on tree branches smoking a large pipe. Tikbalang: A half-man, half-horse creature that misleads travelers in the woods. Tiyanak: A demon-infant that mimics the cries of a real baby to trick wayfarers. Duwende & Nuno sa Punso: Small earth dwarfs or goblins living in mounds and yards. Bathala: The supreme deity in Tagalog mythology. Bakunawa: A giant serpent-like dragon from Visayan mythology believed to swallow the moon, causing eclipses. Hinilawod: An ancient epic poem from Panay following the adventures of demigod brothers like Labaw Donggon.

title: Nigerian Lore
originalText: Yoruba Cosmology: Centers on Ile-Ife as the cradle of creation, featuring deities ( Orishas ) like Obatala (shaper of humanity), Shango (the god of thunder), and Oshun (goddess of river and fertility). Igbo Mythology: Focuses on Chukwu (the supreme creator) and Ala (the powerful Earth goddess of morality and fertility), often utilizing rich proverb cycles and folk wisdom. Hausa Epics: Comprises northern legends and historical myths, such as the heroic foundation story of the Queen of Daura.

title: Algerian Lore
originalText: The Ghoul (or Ogress): A classic shape-shifting monster of North African folklore, often portrayed as a blind or trickster creature inhabiting remote areas. Errouhbani : Forest-dwelling shape-shifter spirits in Berber folklore known for playing pranks on humans. Bouberrak : A traditional folkloric entity associated with sleep paralysis and heavy pressure on the chest. The Blacksmith’s Daughter: A famous Berber-infused traditional tale where a humble smith's daughter marries a prince, gives birth to celestial-marked children, and overcomes palace jealousy. The Seven Brothers and Their Sister (Yasmina): A tale of immense sacrifice and disciplined silence where a sister must weave shirts out of stinging nettles without speaking a word to break a bird-curse on her brothers. The Blue Jackal: A popular animal fable about a jackal who dyes himself blue, tricks the other animals into obeying him, but ultimately falls to arrogance when exposure to rain washes away his disguise.

title: Chile Lore
originalText: The North (Atacama & Andes) Alicanto : A magical, nocturnal bird that feeds on gold and silver ore. Its wings glow brilliantly in the dark. Miners follow it to strike it rich, but if they get greedy, the bird turns off its light and abandons them in the desert. La Tirana: A legendary festival honoring an Inca princess who fell in love with a Spanish priest. It remains one of Chile's biggest religious celebrations . El Chonchón : A severed, flying human head. Its ears grow into massive wings that allow it to soar through the night sky, bringing bad luck or death to those who hear its screech. Pedro Urdemales: The ultimate Chilean folk trickster. Originating from Spanish tales but localized in Chile, he is a clever folk hero who outwits wealthy landowners, priests, and even the devil. La Pincoya : A breathtakingly beautiful ocean goddess who protects the sea and rescues lost fishermen. Her dance on the beach indicates the ocean's bounty; if she faces the sea, fishing will be abundant, but if she faces the shore, a food shortage is coming. El Trauco : A short, deformed dwarf living in the deep southern forests. He carries a stone axe and possesses a hypnotic, magnetic gaze that no woman can resist, making him a fixture in local origin stories. El Caleuche : A mythical, glowing ghost ship crewed by drowned fishermen and sorcerers. It travels invisibly through the fog, hosting vibrant parties at night, and is believed to transport the souls of the ocean bound. La Cueca: Chile's national dance. It is a flirtatious, courtship dance between a man and a woman who wave white handkerchiefs, representing the interactions between a rooster and a hen. Trova & Canto Nuevo: Musical styles deeply rooted in rural farm life and urban social movements, famously using instruments like the guitarra , guitarrón chileno , and pandero .

title: Iranian Lore
originalText: ranian folklore and mythology is a rich tapestry of epic heroism, cosmic battles between light and darkness, and chilling supernatural creatures passed down through thousands of years. Much of these traditional tales originate from the Zoroastrian holy book, the Avesta , and are immortalized in the Shahnameh (Book of Kings). [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] At the heart of Iranian mythology is the eternal battle between Ahura Mazda (the Wise Lord of creation, light, and truth) and Angra Mainyu/Ahriman (the destructive spirit of darkness and evil). Other major deities include Mithra (god of the sun, truth, and covenants) and Anahita (goddess of water and fertility). The Shahnameh blends history and myth, following the lives of Persia's greatest warriors and kings: Rostam: The ultimate Persian champion. He rides the magical, intelligent horse Rakhsh and is aided by the Simurgh , a benevolent, wise bird resembling a phoenix with the head of a dog and the claws of a lion. Zahhak: A tyrannical king with two snake-shoulders that sprouted after being kissed by the devil, requiring him to feed human brains to the serpents every day. Kaveh the Blacksmith: A legendary figure who led an uprising against Zahhak using his blacksmith's apron as a revolutionary flag (the Derafsh Kaviani ). Mythical Beasts and Spirits Iranian folklore is populated by a wide array of creatures, fairies, and monsters: [ 1 ] Deevs: Malevolent giants or demons, often depicted with horns and massive strength, who serve as the primary antagonists in heroic tales. Aal: A terrifying demon resembling a scrawny old woman with long, iron-like claws and fire in her eyes. Folklore warns that she preys on pregnant women and newborns. Pari: Beautiful, winged, fairy-like spirits that act as guides or helpers to humans, occupying a middle ground between angels and demons. Sang-e Sabur (The Patient Stone): A magical, empathetic stone that listens to the deepest sorrows and secrets of the person holding it. It is believed to absorb the trauma until it eventually bursts into pieces from the weight of grief. The Fortune Teller of Old: Folktales often feature cunning tricksters, wise old women (such as Pirezan ), and genies ( Jinn ) that interact with mortals in the desert or remote mountain villages.

title: Turkmenistan Lore
originalText: Gorogly ( Görogly ): The grand national epic detailing the heroic deeds of Gorogly and his 40 horsemen, filled with hundreds of traditional songs and values of courage and loyalty. Destans : Oral historical compositions that blend poetry, romance, fairy tales, and moral codes, traditionally chanted to listeners. Oghuz Khan Legend: The foundational origin myth tracing the lineage of Turkmen tribes back to Oghuz Khan. Bakhshi: Revered itinerant bard-minstrels who travel from village to village preserving history and reciting epics from memory. Dutar: A two-stringed long-necked lute considered the soulful heart of Turkmen musical folklore Tuyduk & Rituals: Traditional flutes linked in folklore to creation myths involving Adam, accompanied by symbolic circular shamanistic movements. Ependi (Khoja Nasreddin): Beloved humorous and wise folkloric character whose witty anecdotes teach moral lessons. Magtymguly & Kemine Cycles: Folk tales and satirical jokes built around historical classical poets and local wits. Superstitions and Creatures: Beliefs in protective charms against the evil eye, alongside legendary beings like the Tulpar (winged horse) and forest spirits

title: Lesotho Lore
originalText: Khodumodumo (or Khanyapa): A massive, gluttonous monster that swallowed every human and animal in its path. In the epic tale of Ditaolane, only one woman survived by hiding in ashes, and she gave birth to a miraculous boy who eventually cut the monster open to free the swallowed villagers. [ 1 , 2 ] Monyohe: The Great Water Snake. Monyohe is deeply tied to the landscape of Lesotho, symbolizing fertility, procreation, and rainfall. In many tales, a chief’s daughter must marry the snake to restore access to water during severe droughts. Nanabolele: A bioluminescent, reptilian creature that glows in the dark like stars and lives in deep waters. Its hide is considered incredibly valuable and deadly. 'Mutla (The Hare): The ultimate trickster. 'Mutla constantly outsmarts larger predators like the wolf or jackal through quick thinking and deception. The Talking Bird: A motif found in tales like Masilo and Marcelon . When a greedy brother murders the other for a miraculous cow, a talking bird trails him back to the village and exposes his crimes to the villagers. Storytelling ( Ts'omo ): Folktales were traditionally told in the evening around the fire. They are highly interactive, often featuring songs and choruses that the audience—typically children—must sing to help the story progress. The Origin of the Mokorotlo: Lesotho's iconic, conical straw hat is said to have been designed in the shape of Qiloane Mountain, a prominent peak near the historic fortress of Thaba Bosiu.

title: Bangladesh Lore
originalText: Manasamangal : An epic centered on the snake goddess Manasa and the unmatched devotion and grit of human heroine Behula . Mymensingh Gitika: A famous collection of romantic folk ballads featuring tragic local love stories like Malua and Mahua . Nath Geetika: Oral poems detailing the spiritual transformations and trials of historic figures like Prince Gopi Chandra . Baul Tradition: A mystical, lyric-driven genre of wandering minstrels focused on divine love within. Bhatiali & Bhawaiya : Boatmen's and pastoral melodies reflecting longing, separation, and the rhythms of the rivers. Gambhira: A dramatic narrative folk performance traditionally utilizing a grand-uncle and grandson dialogue to blend satire and social commentary. Nishir Daak: A phantom nighttime voice calling out a person’s name; answering it is believed to lead to disappearance. Aleya: Mysterious, flickering ghost lights seen over marshes, believed to be the wandering souls of the drowned. Khona’s Sayings: Traditional agricultural and meteorological rhyming couplets by the legendary female astronomer Khona , still used to guide crop planting. Thakumar Jhuli : The classic compilation of grandmother's fairy tales filled with magic, talking animals, and mythical creatures collected by Dakshinaranjan Mitra Majumdar .

title: Estonia Lore
originalText: Early Estonian mythology was deeply connected to the environment, featuring sacred groves ( hiis ), springs, and erratics . [ 1 ] Taara: The supreme god of nature, primarily worshipped by the Oeselians (people of Saaremaa). Tharapita : A warlike god, said to have been born on a mountain in Virumaa in northern Estonia. Lindu : The daughter of the sky god Uko , who cared for the birds and migrated them; she became the Milky Way. Kalevipoeg: The national epic, compiled by Friedrich Reinhold Kreutzwald. It follows the giant Kalevipoeg, who performs superhuman feats of strength, battles the devil, and serves as the defender of the land. Suur Tõll: A giant and legendary protector of the island of Saaremaa, known for defending his people from enemies and even fighting the devil. Estonian folklore includes a spirit or haldjas for virtually every element of the natural world. Kratt (or Tulihänd / Pisuhänd ): A magical servant made from straw or household tools and brought to life through a drop of the creator’s blood and a deal with the devil. It travels as a fiery serpent or dragon to steal grain and treasures for its master. It must be kept constantly busy, otherwise it will turn on its creator. Vanapagan : Literally meaning "the old pagan." He is a clever, yet highly gullible and malicious devil figure who is frequently outsmarted by peasants in comic tales. Näkk : A dangerous shapeshifting water spirit that haunts rivers and lakes, often luring victims into the water with music. Metsaema and Metsaisa : The forest mother and father who govern the woods and its wildlife. Estonian folk music and poetry are famous for the regilaul (runic songs). These ancient, monophonic, and unrhymed folk songs were historically chanted by choirs in call-and-response form. They cover every aspect of life—from work and weddings to calendar holidays—and the Estonian folklore archives house over 133,000 recorded songs.

title: Bolivia Lore
originalText: Pachamama: The supreme Mother Earth goddess, revered across the Andean region. Bolivians perform daily rituals to her, such as " challa ," which involves pouring a few drops of alcohol or burying symbolic objects before drinking or building. El Tío : The legendary guardian spirit and "devil" of the mines. Miners in places like Potosí leave offerings of cigarettes, coca leaves, and alcohol to El Tío in exchange for protection and rich veins of ore. Tunupa / The Mountains: In the southern altiplano , Tunupa is a mythic heroine who shaped the Andean landscape. Mountains like Illimani and Illampu are often personified as jealous warriors fighting over her, whose tears formed the landscape and the multi-colored kantuta flower. Carnaval de Oruro: An epic UNESCO-recognized festival where thousands of dancers perform indigenous and colonial dances. La Diablada (Dance of the Devils): Originating in Oruro, this dance features elaborate, terrifying devil masks and represents the triumph of good over evil. Caporales : An energetic, modern folk dance based on the Afro-Bolivian Saya . Dancers wear jingling bells and bright velvet costumes, reenacting the movements of historic colonial ranch overseers. Phujllay : A satirical, celebratory dance from Tarabuco that celebrates Indigenous courage and mocks Spanish Conquistadors by having dancers wear large, helmet-like hats. Salar de Uyuni: The vast salt flats are said to be the result of a massive flood sent by the creator god Viracocha, or are alternatively tied to the tears of the goddess Tunupa . Lake Titicaca: Legend dictates the sun and moon rose from this lake. It was also the birthplace of Manco Capac and Mama Ocllo, the founders of the Incan Empire. El Toborochi : A Guarani legend tells the tale of Araverá , a woman who hid inside the amphora-shaped trunk of a toborochi tree. The tree blooms into a beautiful flower as her spirit comes out to attract hummingbirds. Alasitas Fair: Held annually in La Paz, this festival honors Ekeko , the god of abundance. People buy miniature items (like tiny cars, money, or houses) hoping Ekeko will bless them with the real things in the coming year.

title: Brazilian Lore
originalText: Saci- Pererê : A famous, mischievous one-legged Black boy who smokes a pipe and wears a red cap. He travels inside mini-whirlwinds, hiding in the woods to play tricks on farmers and travelers. Curupira : A jungle spirit recognized by his bright red hair and backwards-facing feet. He uses his backward tracks to confuse hunters and protect the forests. Iara: The Amazonian siren. A beautiful, half-human, half-fish water spirit who sings enchanting melodies to lure men into the rivers. Boto Cor-de-Rosa (The Pink Dolphin): Originating from the Amazon, this legend claims that pink dolphins transform into handsome, well-dressed men during the nighttime to seduce local women. Boitatá : A giant, fiery serpent or dragon with glowing eyes that acts as a fierce protector of the Amazon, targeting those who start forest fires. Mula sem Cabeça (Headless Mule): A terrifying creature in the form of a mule with flames bursting from its neck, which thunders through the fields to punish those who break moral codes. Cuca: A fearsome, alligator-like witch with long blond hair who steals and curses disobedient children.

title: Nebraska Lore
originalText: Key Legends and Figures The Alkali Lake Monster: Lurking in Walgren Lake near Hay Springs, this cryptid was first reported in 1923. Witnesses described a massive, gray-olive, long-necked beast with four flippers and a toothy snout. Febold Feboldson: Originating in Gothenburg, this folk hero was a Swedish plainsman known for his superhuman abilities, like "cloudbusting" to cure droughts and inventing creative ways to battle extreme prairie weather. Antonine Barada: A legendary figure often compared to Paul Bunyan, Barada was a mix-raced (Omaha and French) strongman from the Nebraska Territory known for his immense physical power and bravery. Weeping Water Legend: According to Pawnee and Otoe folklore, the creek got its tragic name from the tears of Indigenous maidens who wept endlessly after the loss of their lovers in a tribal battle. Spooky Tales and Urban Legends Hummel Park Albinos (Omaha): A persistent Omaha urban legend centers on Hummel Park, where tales of pale, albino humanoids roaming the wooded trails and sewers have been passed down for decades. The Salt Witch (Lincoln): Legend holds that a witch associated with the Lincoln salt basins cursed the area's water and early settlers, explaining the saline nature of the land and causing eerie events around the capital. Mutant Radioactive Hornets (Central Nebraska): Following the 2011 Fukushima disaster, a bizarre urban legend circulated in 2013 that giant, highly aggressive radioactive hornets had infested central Nebraska, sporting venom thousands of times stronger than normal wasps. Indigenous Roots Nebraska's folklore is deeply rooted in the traditions of the Plains tribes, including the Pawnee, Omaha, Otoe-Missouria, and Lakota. These myths often explain the creation of natural phenomena, feature trickster characters like the rabbit or coyote, and highlight traditional moral lessons and spiritual customs.

title: Kentucky Lore
originalText: K entucky folklore is a rich tapestry of Appalachian oral traditions, tall tales, and haunted history. It features legendary cryptids like the half-man, half-goat Pope Lick Monster and the spectral Sleepy Hollow Hearse , rooted deeply in the rugged hollows and rolling landscapes of the Bluegrass State. Rooted heavily in Appalachian culture, the folklore reflects the state's geography and historical mysteries. Cryptids: the Pope Lick Monster that lures people to railroad trestles in Louisville, and persistent sightings of Appalachian Black Panthers . [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] Haunted Roads: Spooky driving routes like Sleepy Hollow Road (where a ghost hearse attempts to run drivers off the road) and Crybaby Bridges are local staples. Tall Tales: The storytelling tradition thrives on exaggerated historical figures like Daniel Boone and tales surrounding Kentucky's infamous moonshiners.

title: Hawaii Lore
originalText: awaiian folklore is a rich oral tradition of myths, legends, and chants that explain the creation of the world, the origins of natural phenomena, and the moral codes of the Kanaka Maoli (Native Hawaiians). At its core are deeply respected deities, environmental guardians, and strict cultural taboos (kapu). Major Deities and Demigods The Hawaiian pantheon is vast, but several figures are central to the islands' storytelling. Pele : The passionate and volatile goddess of fire and volcanoes. She is said to reside in Halema ʻ uma ʻ u crater at the summit of Kilauea on the Big Island. Māui : A shapeshifting demigod known throughout Polynesia. In Hawaiian legend, he famously used a giant fishhook to pull the islands from the ocean and lassoed the sun to slow its path and lengthen the days. Kamapua ʻ a : A fierce, shape-shifting demigod who can take the form of a hog, a fish, or a plant. He is known for his tempestuous and passionate romantic rivalry with the goddess Pele. Spirit Guardians and Mythical Figures The Hawaiian landscape is alive with spirits and supernatural entities that watch over the land and sea. Menehune : A legendary race of small, skilled craftspeople who live deep in the forests and valleys. They are renowned for building incredible structures—such as the Alekoko Fishpond on Kaua ʻ i — over the course of a single night. Mo ʻ o : Shapeshifting lizard or dragon-like water spirits that serve as the guardians of streams, waterfalls, and fishponds. They control the flow of water and punish those who pollute the land. ʻ Aumākua : Personal or family gods that often take the form of animals like the honu (turtle), pueo (owl), or manō (shark). They serve as spiritual guides and protectors of the family lineage. Superstitions and Unwritten Rules Certain traditions and taboos are highly respected by both locals and visitors out of reverence for the land and past spirits. The Night Marchers ( Huaka ʻ i P ō ) : The spirits of ancient, high-ranking chiefs and warriors who march across the islands at night. Legend warns that if you encounter them, you must lie flat on the ground facedown to avoid making eye contact. The Pali Highway Pork Taboo : According to local folklore, you should never carry pork across the Pali Highway connecting Honolulu to Windward O ʻ ahu. The legend stems from the bitter separation of Pele and the hog-demigod Kamapua ʻ a . The Naupaka Flower : A sad love story explaining the half-petaled white flowers found in the mountains and on the beach. Two lovers were forbidden to be together by the gods, tearing the flower in half, leaving one half for the mountains and the other for the sea.

title: New Jersey Lore
originalText: New Jersey's folklore is rich with cryptids, ghosts, and eerie mysteries. The crown jewel is the Jersey Devil , a winged, hooved beast said to terrorize the 1-million-acre Pine Barrens . Legend claims Mother Leeds cursed her 13th child in 1735, causing the baby to transform into a monster and fly away into the swamps. Other notable Garden State legends include: Clinton Road (Passaic County): Known as one of the most haunted roads in America. Folklore includes tales of a ghost boy on the bridge who returns coins dropped into the water, phantom vehicles, and connections to mafia body-dumping. The Blue Hole (Winslow): A deep, eerie, indigo-colored pond in the Pine Barrens. Local mythology claims it has no bottom, acts as a vortex, and is home to the Jersey Devil or other sinister water spirits. The Pig Lady of Mount Misery (Burlington County): A haunting spirit tied to "Pig Lady Road," said to be the ghost of a woman who roams the isolated woods seeking revenge for brutal ax attacks. The Black Doctor of the Pines: The spirit of James Still, a 19th-century self-taught African American herbalist who lived in the Pine Barrens. Legend says his ghost still appears to aid lost or injured travelers.

title: South Carolina Lore
originalText: Cryptids & Monsters The Lizard Man: A 7-foot-tall reptilian creature with searing red eyes and three-clawed fingers, first sighted in Lee County in 1988 after it allegedly attacked a teenager's car. Third-Eye Man: A phantom reported by students in 1949 who claimed to see a man with an extra eye roaming the "catacombs" beneath the University of South Carolina in Columbia. Hound of Goshen: A spectral "happy dog" that reportedly tracks down the killers of its owner through Union and Newberry counties. Ghostly Phenomena The Gray Man: A ghostly figure seen wandering Pawleys Island before major hurricanes; seeing him is said to spare your home from the worst of the storm's destruction. The Ravenel Lights: Mysterious, otherworldly lights that appear near ancient Baptist churches and train tracks in Ravenel, sometimes accompanied by strange winds and hand-shaped dents on nearby cars. Old State Road Legends: In Cayce, a local urban legend claims that if you put flour on your car bumper and stop on the railroad tracks past a church, ghostly handprints will appear to push your car to safety. Gullah & Coastal Folklore Boo Hags: From Gullah mythology, these are skinless spirits that steal human breath and ride horses at night. They can be warded off by putting salt or brooms with many bristles by your doorways. Blue Bottle Trees: Used across the South Carolina lowlands, placing blue glass bottles on branches is a Gullah tradition meant to trap evil spirits or "hags" that come out at night. Dr. Buzzard: A well-known historical figure and voodoo doctor from St. Helena Island who used roots, herbs, and hexes to practice hoodoo. Historical Haunts & Curses Lands End Ghost: A legendary figure who wanders the Sea Islands of South Carolina, usually spotted walking along coastal roads. Julia Legare: An Edisto Island legend of a woman mistakenly buried alive. Her tomb was sealed, but later found open from the inside, with handprints remaining on the mausoleum doors for years. Old Exchange Dungeon: In Charleston, this colonial-era prison is famously haunted by the ghosts of pirates, prisoners, and British soldiers from the American Revolution.

title: Oregon Lore
originalText: Native American oral histories describe a massive natural rock arch across the Columbia River that was destroyed by the gods, forming the Cascade Rapids. Geologists confirm this story aligns with the prehistoric Bonneville Landslide. Crater L ake The Klamath tribe tells of a catastrophic war between Llao (the chief of the below-world) and Skell (the chief of the above-world), which resulted in the collapse of Mount Mazama and the creation of Crater Lake. Wizard Island Bridge of the Gods: Cryptids & Monsters Bigfoot: Oregon is a global epicenter for Bigfoot (Sasquatch) lore. The Pacific Northwest forests—particularly the remote areas around the Cascade Range and the Coast Range—are the most heavily reported regions for sightings. Wallowa Lake Monster: Eastern Oregon's Wallowa Lake is home to "Wally," a creature described since 1885 as a 100-foot-long beast with a hippo-like head. Colossal Claude: A 40-foot serpent-like monster historically spotted by sailors and locals at the mouth of the Columbia River. The Agropelter: A mischievous, long-limbed creature from lumberjack folklore that hurls heavy tree branches at woodsmen. Spooky Lore & The Unexplained Portland’s Shanghai Tunnels OpenOld Town A network of underground passages beneath the city's Old Town/Chinatown. Urban legend claims they were used by 19th-century saloon keepers to kidnap or "shanghai" unsuspecting men, forcing them to work on sailing vessels. Tillamook Rock Lighthouse Standing over a mile off the coast, "Terrible Tilly" is the subject of numerous ghost stories and shipwreck tragedies. LaFayette Witch's Curse A woman accused of witchcraft in the 1880s reportedly cursed the town of LaFayette, Oregon, as she died. Soon after, the town's courthouse and several businesses burned down. wandering spirit lights and ghost lanterns associated with pioneer graves along the Mount Hood route

title: New York Lore
originalText: Urban Legends & NYC Folklore The Van der Voort Sisters: The ghosts of two sisters who died in 1880 are said to haunt Central Park’s Wollman Rink , gleefully ice-skating in red and purple dresses without their feet ever touching the ice. The Mole People: An urban legend describing uncontacted communities, said to live in the abandoned subway tunnels and sprawling sewer systems beneath New York City. Staten Island Boat Race: A popular myth claims the ownership of Staten Island was decided by a 24-hour boat race around the island, won by sea captain Christopher Billop. Upstate Haunts & Cryptids The Headless Horseman: Washington Irving’s legendary tal e is rooted in regional Dutch ghost stories and rumors of a phantom Revolutionary War soldier. Champ (Lake Champlain Monster): Often described as a long, serpent-like cryptid with horns, this friendly water monster is said to inhabit Lake Champlain in upstate New York. Fort Niagara Hobgoblin & Henri the Headless: At Old Fort Niag a ra in Youngstown, the ghost of a French soldier named Henri is said to wander the basement wells searching for his head, alongside a mischievous hobgoblin. Unexplained Phenomena The White Lady of Durand Eastman Park: Found in Rochester, local tales claim the ghost of a grieving mother wanders , searching for her missing daughter. The Marysburgh Vortex: Known as a watery graveyard for shipwrecks, this area of eastern Lake Ontario is fraught with legends of strange disappearances and supernatural turbulence.

title: North Carolina Lore
originalText: Coastal & Pirate Legends The Lost Colony (Dare County): In 1587, the first English settlement in the Americas was established on Roanoke Island. Three years later, when governor John White returned with supplies, the colony had vanished, leaving only the word "CROATOAN" carved into a post. Blackbeard’s Ghost (Ocracoke Island): The infamous pirate Edward Teach (Blackbeard) roamed the Carolina coast and had a hideout at "Teach's Hole." Legend says his headless ghost still swims the waters searching for his severed head, and the mysterious "Maco Light" train apparition haunts the nearby tracks. Mermaid Point (Cape Fear): Local lore tells of mermaids and sea nymphs who rescued sailors and fishermen along the treacherous Cape Fear coastline. Appalachian Mountain Folklore The Brown Mountain Lights: For centuries, mysterious, unexplainable glowing orbs have been seen dancing above the ridges of Brown Mountain. Local Cherokee legend claims they are the torches of grieving maidens. Fairy Crosses (Blue Ridge): Known geologically as staurolite, these rare cross-shaped crystals are said to be the tears of Cherokee fairies who wept when forced to leave their ancestral homelands. The Boojum: A towering, hairy, and greedy monster that roams the Balsam Mountains, stealing food and kidnapping humans. The Moon-Eyed People: A race of small, pale, bearded humanoids who lived in the mountains and could only see at night. They are said to have built ancient structures before being driven out by the Cherokee. Piedmont & Central Lore The Devil's Tramping Ground (Chatham County): A perfect, barren 40-foot circle in the woods where vegetation refuses to grow. Local legend claims the Devil comes here at night to pace in a circle and plot evil. The Beast of Bladenboro (Bladen County): A mysterious creature that terrorized the area in the 1950s, mysteriously slaughtering dogs and livestock. Lydia, the Phantom Hitchhiker: A famous ghost story of a young woman in white who is picked up on Highway 70 near Jamestown, only to vanish before reaching her destination, which is always near a local cemetery. Indigenous & Tall Tales The Cherokee Yellow Jacket (U'lag'û): A massive bird-like monster the size of a house that roamed the Nantahala River and snatched children, eventually trapped by the Cherokee people in a smoky cave. Jack Tales: Brought over by European settlers but adapted to the Appalachian mountains, these are tall tales and magical adventures starring a clever, ever-capable boy named Jack.

title: Wisconsin Lore
originalText: 1. Cryptids & Monsters The Hodag (Rhinelander): Wisconsin’s most famous folklore creature. It has the head of a frog, the face of an elephant, a dinosaur's back, and spears on its tail. It is still the beloved mascot of Rhinelander today. The Beast of Bray Road (Elkhorn): Since the late 1980s, drivers in rural Walworth County have reported seeing a large, fur-covered, wolf-like humanoid walking on its hind legs. The Wendigo: Rooted in Ojibwe and Ho-Chunk Native American traditions, this fearsome, gaunt ice giant embodies insatiable greed and cannibalism, said to stalk the deep Northwoods and Madeline Island. The Wisconsin Manbat : Also known as the Lake Michigan Mothman , this cryptid has been reported in areas like Kenosha, taking the form of a large gargoyle or winged entity. 2. Haunted Locations & Ghost Lore The Pfister Hotel Known as one of the most famously haunted hotels in America, it is often cited by visiting Major League Baseball players who claim to experience unexplained noises, flickering lights, and apparitions in their rooms. The Witch's Tower Also known as the Starin Park water tower, this stone structure is a focal point of local legends, which claim the area is a center for the occult and the site of a buried "witches' circle." Death Song Cave A chilling Winnebago (Ho-Chunk) legend about a cave near the Wisconsin River. Warriors and hunters who entered the cave vanished, accompanied by a strange, mournful melody. 3. Lumberjack & Cultural Tall Tales Before it became the Dairy State, Wisconsin was the "mother of all circuses" and a hub for lumbering. Lumberjack "Fearsome Critters": Loggers in Wisconsin camps entertained themselves with tales of bizarre animals, such as the Hidebehind (a sneaky creature that hides behind tree trunks), the Hodag itself, and the Agropelter (which hurls branches at passersby). Paul Bunyan: Many of the tales surrounding this legendary lumberjack were popularized in Wisconsin logging camps.

title: Mississippi Lore
originalText: The Yazoo Witch (Yazoo City) One of the most enduring ghost legends in the state centers on a "witch" who lived along the Yazoo River. According to legend, a vengeful old woman who lured fishermen to their doom was cornered in 1884 by the local sheriff. Before sinking into the quicksand and dying, she supposedly cursed the town, warning she would return in 20 years. Her grave in Glenwood Cemetery is infamous for its heavy, broken iron chains, which locals claim hold her spirit in check. Exactly twenty years later, in 1904, a massive, mysterious fire swept through Yazoo City, destroying over 300 buildings. The Devil at the Crossroads (Clarksdale) Mississippi is widely celebrated as the birthplace of the Delta Blues, and with it comes one of the most famous musical urban legends in the United States. Legend holds that blues pioneer Robert Johnson took his guitar to a desolate crossroads in Clarksdale, Mississippi, at midnight and sold his soul to the devil in exchange for unprecedented musical talent. This supernatural tale has become a massive cornerstone of both American folklore and blues history. The Witch's Dance (Natchez Trace) Located south of Tupelo off the Natchez Trace Parkway, the "Witch's Dance" is a wooded area that local folklore claims was a ceremonial gathering place for witches in the late 1700s. Legends suggested that the ground where the witches danced turned black, and nothing would ever grow there. The site's ominous reputation was even documented by Andrew Jackson in his journal, who noted the cursed, barren soil. Haunted Locations & Ghosts King's Tavern (Natchez): Dating back to 1789, this structure is the oldest standing building in Natchez. Folklore claims it is haunted by Meline, a mistress of the tavern's original owner who was reportedly murdered and walled up in the tavern's cellar, as well as by the notorious, red-haired Harp brothers, who were early 19th-century bandits. [ 1 ] McRaven House (Vicksburg): Known as "Mississippi's Most Haunted House," the grounds served as a Confederate campsite and field hospital. At least eleven Confederate soldiers are reportedly buried on the property, and the ghost of Mary Elizabeth Howard—who died in the home in 1836—is said to be highly active. Cryptids and River Myths The Three-Legged Woman of Nash Road (Columbus): Legend states that if you drive down Nash Road at night and turn off your car, a phantom three-legged woman will appear. The Pascagoula River Mermaid: Along the Gulf Coast, the Pascagoula River—also known as the "Singing River"—is famous for a Native American legend about a group of local Pascagoula tribes who chose to march into the river and drown themselves singing, rather than face enslavement by a hostile tribe. Some variations of the lore include sightings of a siren or mermaid figure.

title: Minnesota Lore
originalText: The Logging Era and Tall Tales Paul Bunyan & Babe the Blue Ox: The legendary giant lumberjack and his massive blue companion are heavily tied to Minnesota. While popularized by early 20th-century journalists, you can see massive 26-foot and 10-foot statues of the duo standing outside the Bemidji Tourist Information Center in northern Minnesota. Cordwood Pete: The fictional, smaller brother of Paul Bunyan who primarily chopped cordwood around Fosston, Minnesota. Indigenous Legends and Cryptids The Wendigo: Originating in Ojibwe and Algonquin lore, this tall, gaunt, and terrifying spirit embodies greed, famine, and cannibalism. Deeply feared in the isolated winter wilderness, it remains one of the most famous cryptids in northern Minnesota. Lake Pepin Serpent (“ Pepie ”): The Mississippi River has its own version of the Loch Ness monster. Sightings of a 30-foot serpentine creature in Lake Pepin date back to the late 1800s, fueling local tourism in nearby towns like Lake City. Other Cryptids: Deep northern swamps and forests are still hotbeds for reported cryptids, including Bigfoot near Two Harbors and dogmen sightings throughout the Chippewa National Forest.

title: Iowa Lore
originalText: Cryptids & Monsters The Van Meter Visitor: In 1903, residents of Van Meter reported encounters with a winged, half-human, half-bat monster that emitted a horrible stench and shot a blinding light from a horn on its forehead. [ 1 , 2 ] Pepie : The legend of a lake monster, similar to Nessie, living in the deep waters of West Okoboji Lake in northwest Iowa. The Ioway Monster Tales: Indigenous folklore, specifically from the Ioway ( Baxoje ) people, includes mythical figures like Sharp-Elbows (a man-eating ogre) and Shunka Warak'in (a wolf-like monster). Ghost Stories & Urban Legends The Children of Iron Hill: Legend claims a fiery train crash in the early 1900s killed orphaned children traveling through Charles City. Today, locals and visitors along the Charlie Western Trail report hearing the cries of children and seeing ghostly figures in the woods. The Mathias Ham House: Built in 1856 in Dubuque, this documented historic site is famous for tales of flickering lights, cold breezes, and the sound of an unplayed organ. Historical Folklore Kate Shelley: One of Iowa’s most celebrated real-life folklore heroes. In 1881, a 15-year-old girl named Kate Shelley crawled across a flooded, storm-ravaged railroad trestle to warn an oncoming passenger train of a collapsed bridge near Moingona , saving countless lives.

title: South Dakota Lore
originalText: Indigenous & Lakota Legend The White Buffalo Calf Woman A cornerstone of Lakota lore . According to tradition tied to Wind Cave near Hot Springs, she brought the sacred pipe and ceremonies to the people, promising abundance. Sica Hollow Located in northeastern South Dakota, this heavily forested ravine was deemed sacred and "evil" by the Sioux (meaning they refused to hunt there) due to its crimson-running water. A Dakota legend tells of a young boy who spotted enemies disguised as wolves. The warriors avenged the women and children by trapping and defeating the enemies in this exact lake. Cryptids & Spooky Folklore The Badlands Banshee: A wailing ghost haunting the rugged, eroded terrain of the Badlands. Walking Sam: A shadowy, tall, and thin figure who stalks the Black Hills. The Jackalope: T his mythical horned rabbit is famously celebrated as a plains "fearsome critter" from the Dakota frontier. Wild West Legends & Outlaws Jesse James and Devil's Gulch: Located in Garretson, this 60-foot canyon is the site where the notorious outlaw Jesse James reportedly leapt his horse across an 18-foot gap to evade a posse . Potato Creek Johnny: A famed local folk hero and prospector of the Black Hills who discovered one of the largest gold nuggets in the region (7.5 troy ounces) in 1929. He is buried in Deadwood's Mount Moriah Cemetery (cityofdeadwood.com). [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] Hugh Glass: The ultimate frontier survival legend. Attacked by a grizzly bear along the Grand River, he famously crawled hundreds of miles across the South Dakota wilderness to seek revenge on the trappers who abandoned him. Geographical Tall Tales Paul Bunyan in the Black Hills: Logging tall tales place the giant lumberjack Paul Bunyan in the Dakotas, claiming he and his blue ox Babe traversed the state and created the Black Hills. Spirit Mound: Located near Vermillion, early legends told of tiny, protective creatures living here, a place Lewis and Clark visited in 1804 when investigating the mound. The exact location and visiting hours for Mount Moriah Cemetery.

title: New Mexico Lore
originalText: 1. La Llorona (The Weeping Woman) Deeply embedded in the Hispanic oral tradition across the state, this spirit is a tragic mother who drowned her own children in a fit of jealousy. She is said to perpetually roam the rushing waters of the Rio Grande and the Pecos River, clad in a flowing white dress and loudly crying out for her lost children. 2. Skinwalkers Derived from Navajo traditions, skinwalkers ( yee naaldlooshii ) are human witches who have attained dark, supernatural powers. They are capable of shape-shifting into animals like coyotes, wolves, owls, or crows, and are known for their terrifying, glowing eyes and uncanny speed. 3. Brujas (Witches) New Mexican colonial history is filled with legends of brujas . Folklorist accounts note stories of witches who could make themselves invisible or even shape-shift into owls. Local superstitions warn that if you see a tecolote (owl) in a tree and it asks for salt the following day, you have encountered a witch. 4. The Taos Hum Located in the northern region of the state, the Taos Hum is a persistent, low-frequency buzzing noise that a small percentage of residents and visitors claim to hear. Despite scientific investigations, its exact origin remains completely unexplained. 5. The Roswell Incident New Mexico is an international hub for UFO and alien lore, anchored by the infamous events of July 1947. While the military claimed a weather balloon crashed, local folklore and global conspiracy theories continue to insist that an extraterrestrial spacecraft and its alien crew were recovered near Roswell.

title: Illinois Lore
originalText: Illinois folklore is a rich, spooky tapestry woven from Native American mythology, French exploration, and Midwestern urban legends. Spanning from the deep south to Chicago, it blends tales of ghostly hitchhikers, bizarre cryptids, and haunted historical sites. 👻 Chicago & Northern Ghosts Resurrection Mary: The most famous ghost in Illinois lore. Mary is a young woman in a white dress and dancing shoes who reportedly flags down drivers along Archer Avenue in Justice, Illinois, asking for a ride before vanishing near the gates of Resurrection Cemetery. Bachelor's Grove Cemetery: Tucked away in the Rubio Woods near Midlothian, this abandoned 19th-century graveyard is considered one of the most haunted places in the Midwest, known for phantom vehicles, hovering orbs, and a glowing "vanishing house." Hull House Devil Baby: During the early 1900s, Jane Addams' famous settlement house in Chicago was the epicenter of a rumor about a born-to-human-parents Devil Baby—complete with pointed ears, cloven hooves, and a tail—who was supposedly left on the doorstep and later raised in the attic. 🦖 Cryptids & Monsters The Piasa Bird: One of Illinois' oldest legends, stemming from a massive painting on the bluffs of the Mississippi River near Alton. Documented by French explorers in 1673, it was described by the Illini people as a giant, man-eating, dragon-like bird with the head of a man. Big Muddy Monster: In the early 1970s, the rural woods and river bottoms near Murphysboro (Southern Illinois) were terrorized by sightings of a tall, foul-smelling, hairy cryptid, prompting massive local citizen search parties. The Mad Gasser of Mattoon: In 1944, a series of bizarre attacks swept Mattoon, Illinois, wherein residents reported an invisible assailant spraying a strange, sweet-smelling gas into their bedroom windows, causing temporary paralysis and nausea. 🏚️ Historic & Southern Lore Crenshaw House (The Old Slave House): Located in rural Equality, this notorious 1830s mansion features a third-floor "slave attic". Local folklore insists that owner John Hart Crenshaw used the house to kidnap free African Americans and sell them into slavery, and that the attic still holds the tormented spirits of those imprisoned there. Cato the Witch (Carmi): A localized Southern Illinois legend centered around an early 19th-century woman in Carmi who locals suspected of practicing dark magic and herbal witchcraft. 🪦 Bizarre Curses & Mummies Deaf Bill (Alton): Local lore in Alton recounts the story of "Deaf Bill," a mute, local fisherman who died in the early 1900s. Because his body went unclaimed and the funeral home needed an exhibit to pay for expenses, his mummy was placed in an upright closet in the Bower Funeral Home for eight decades, where neighborhood kids used to dare each other to poke him.

title: Louisiana Lore
originalText: Legendary Creatures & Spirits The Rougarou: Rooted in French loup-garou tales, this shapeshifting, wolf-headed beast is said to hunt the swamps at night. The legend was famously used by parents to keep misbehaving children in line and enforce religious practices like Lent. Feu Follet: Also called fifollet , these are mysterious, glowing orbs of light floating over the marshes. Local lore suggests they represent the spirits of the lost or serve as mischievous tricksters guarding hidden treasure. The Grunch: Exclusive to New Orleans urban legend, these are small, deformed, vampiric creatures that allegedly inhabit the shadowy, overgrown edges of the city. Folk Heroes & Characters Bouki and Lapin: Found deeply in Creole and African-American folktales, Bouki is a dull-witted, gullible hyena/alligator figure, while Lapin (the rabbit) is the clever, wily trickster who always outsmarts him. Traiteurs (Folk Healers): A significant part of Cajun culture, traiteurs are traditional folk healers who utilize prayer, laying on of hands, and herbal remedies to cure ailments. Voodoo & Historical Legends Marie Laveau: The revered, historically documented 19th-century Voodoo Queen of New Orleans. Her legend is surrounded by mysticism, with stories claiming she could heal the sick, cast powerful gris-gris charms, and even influence the weather. Madame LaLaurie Mansion: A notorious New Orleans historical legend. Located in the French Quarter, the 1830s home is tied to tales of severe cruelty committed by Delphine LaLaurie. It is widely considered one of the most haunted sites in the country.

title: Arkansas Lore
originalText: Arkansas folklore weaves together Native American heritage, pioneer tall tales, and rural legends born from the Ozarks and Delta flatlands. Iconic lore includes the Bigfoot-like Fouke Monster, the ghostly Gurdon Lights, and the 1840s "Arkansas Traveler" tale, which famously cemented the state’s musical and cultural identity. Arkansas Cryptids and Monsters The Fouke Monster: Often called the Boggy Creek Monster, this large, foul-smelling, ape-like cryptid has terrorized the swampy woods near Fouke (near Texarkana) since the 1940s. It inspired a series of cult-classic films, starting with The Legend of Boggy Creek in 1972. The White River Monster: Dubbed "Whitey," this river cryptid is said to inhabit the White River in Newport. Descriptions of the creature vary, but it's often reported as having gray, peeling skin and the size of a small car. In 1973, the Arkansas legislature even passed a resolution to protect the monster. The Gowrow: An Ozark-dwelling monster described as a 20-foot-long, wingless dragon with webbed feet, tusks, and a speared tail. First making waves in an 1897 Arkansas Gazette article, it is said to prey on livestock and emit a low, rumbling growl. Mysterious Lights and Hauntings The Gurdon and Dover Lights: Both the Gurdon Lights (seen near railroad tracks in Clark County) and the Dover Lights (observed in the Ozarks) are famous unexplained glowing orbs. Sightings date back decades, and local folklore attributes the orbs to everything from geological gases to the ghosts of beheaded railroad workers or lost Spanish conquistadors. [ 1 ] The Legend of Petit Jean: The most beloved tale in Arkansas tells the story of a young 18th-century French noblewoman who disguised herself as a cabin boy to follow her explorer fiancé to the New World. Upon learning they were to sail further into the wilderness, she became severely ill, revealed her identity, and died on a high mountain. She was buried on the mountain overlooking the river, which is known today as Petit Jean State Park . Classic Folklore and Heritage The Arkansas Traveler: One of the most prominent pieces of 19th-century American folklore. The story goes that a lost, fiddle-playing politician encountered a suspicious, hermit-like mountain man who refused to give directions. The traveler eventually won the man's hospitality and shelter by playing the second half of a folk tune on the fiddle.

title: North Dakota Lore
originalText: The Miniwashitu Originating in Dakota and Mandan oral tradition, the Miniwashitu is a fearsome, red-furred serpent that dwells in the Missouri River near Bismarck. Described as having a single glowing eye, a horn on its forehead, and sharp spines, the creature is tied to violent spring floods and breaking ice. According to legend, merely looking upon the beast in daylight brings certain death within a year. The Tagus Stairway to Hell Perhaps North Dakota’s most infamous urban legend centers on the ghost town of Tagus in Ward County. The site of a former Lutheran church that burned down in 2001, local rumors claimed the ruins were the epicenter of dark cult activities and cannibalism. A mythical "stairway" is said to lie beneath the ashes, leading to the underworld. The Rougarou Shared with French-Canadian and Ojibwe heritage, the Rougarou is a monstrous werewolf-like creature that haunts the Turtle Mountains. Brought to the region by French fur trappers, the beast was famously used by elders to warn children to behave and observe Lent. Wrong Side Up One of the most famous pioneer folktales tells the story of an 1880s settler breaking the pristine prairie sod for wheat. An Indigenous elder watched him plow, picked up a clod of dirt, and told the pioneer he had it "wrong side up" before walking away. The settler laughed, but the legend became a somber truth—turning the native grass under left the topsoil vulnerable to the wind, leading to massive soil erosion in the region.

title: Colorado Lore
originalText: Legendary Creatures The Slide Rock Bolter: A massive, whale-like creature said to inhabit steep mountain slopes in Southwest Colorado. Legend holds it uses a hooked tail to anchor itself to mountain peaks before dropping down to swallow tourists whole. Tommyknockers: Brought by Cornish miners during the Gold Rush, these are mischievous yet superstitious pixie-like entities. Miners believed they lived in the deep, dark underground tunnels, warning men of cave-ins by knocking on the rock walls, or playing tricks if treated disrespectfully. Today, the lore lives on at the Tommyknoocker Brewery in Idaho Springs. Eerie & Haunted Histories Located in Estes Park, this historic hotel is globally famous for inspiring Stephen King’s horror novel, The Shining . It is deeply tied to paranormal folklore, with guests and staff regularly recounting tales of ghostly piano music and apparitions from its early 1900s founders. The Vampire Of Lafayette Buried in the Lafayette Municipal Cemetery, Theodore Glava was an Eastern European coal miner who died during the 1918 influenza pandemic. Local hysteria led to a dark urban legend that he was a vampire, a rumor that was fueled by the bizarre iron cross structure erected over his grave to "keep him down." Cheesman Park is one of Denver’s most beautiful green spaces, but it was established on land that was originally Prospect Hill Cemetery. In the late 1800s, the city tried to relocate the bodies, but a botched, macabre process resulted in thousands of remains being left behind beneath the park grounds. This dark history continues to fuel local ghost stories. Tales from the Western Frontier Silver Heels: A legendary dancehall girl from the 1860s mining camp of Buckskin Joe. According to folklore, she nursed miners through a devastating smallpox outbreak while wearing a mask to hide her pox-scarred face. When the epidemic ended, she disappeared without a trace, and the miners named a mountain peak, Mount Silverheels, in her honor.

title: Maryland Lore
originalText: The Snallygaster Originating in the rural woods of Frederick County, this legendary monster is described as a half-bird, half-reptile chimera with sharp metallic tentacles. The legend traces back to early German immigrants who called it the Schneller Geist (meaning "fast ghost"). In the early 20th century, local newspapers published sensationalized reports of the beast, and it is even rumored that Theodore Roosevelt once intended to travel to Maryland to hunt the creature. Historically, moonshiners in South Mountain cleverly used the terrifying screeches and sightings of the Snallygaster to scare away revenue agents during Prohibition. The Goatman of Prince George's County A prominent urban legend in Maryland is the Goatman . The creature is typically described as a half-man, half-goat mutant—the result of a genetic experiment gone wrong at the Beltsville Agricultural Research Center. The legend gained widespread traction in 1971 following an undergraduate project at the University of Maryland. While the scientific origins are fictional, the lore is partially rooted in a series of local pet disappearances and sightings that terrified the region in the 1970s.

title: Connecticut Lore
originalText: Connecticut folklore is rich with tales of cryptids, haunted locations, and colonial mysteries. Famous legends include the Melon Heads of Milford and the cursed, abandoned town of Dudleytown in Cornwall. The state's deep colonial roots have also inspired enduring stories of New England vampires , notably the 19th-century exhumations linked to the JB55 skeleton. Cryptids and Monsters The Connecticut River Serpent: Nicknamed "Connie," tales of a large sea serpent in the Connecticut River date back to an encounter in 1886 near Cromwell and Middletown. The Higganum Mucket: Originating in Higganum in the 1950s, this aquatic cryptid was historically the subject of local fire department hazing rituals, where recruits were sent to look for the scaly, horned swamp beast. The Glawackus : A legendary, terrifying creature that prompted a massive monster-hunting frenzy in the early 1900s, sighted primarily in the woods of Glastonbury and surrounding towns. Haunted and Cursed Places Dudleytown : Often called the "Village of the Damned," this abandoned Cornwall settlement is infamous for legends of curses, inexplicable tragedies, and hauntings tracing back to its early colonial founders. Melon Heads: Urban legend holds that in-bred descendants of escaped asylum patients roam the wooded backroads of Fairfield County—specifically around Shelton, Trumbull, and Milford—attacking passing cars. Charles Island (Milford): Located off the coast of Silver Sands State Park, this bird sanctuary is said to be thrice-cursed, once by the pirate Captain William Kidd, whose fabled treasure is supposedly buried there. Devil's Hopyard State Park (East Haddam): Legend claims that perfectly round potholes in the rocks at the bottom of the waterfall were scorched by the Devil himself as he stomped across the stones in anger. Historical Superstitions The New England Vampire Panic: During the 18th and 19th centuries, tuberculosis outbreaks led to mass hysteria. Believing that deceased family members were rising from the grave to drain the life of the living, locals would exhume bodies to burn their hearts. The Leatherman: A real-life wandering vagabond from the late 19th century who walked a continuous loop through Connecticut and New York. His legend lives on in local lore through the rock shelters and caves he used for sleep. the abandoned Fairy Village in Middlebury:

title: Alabama Lore
originalText: Alabama’s folklore blends Native American myths, Civil War history, and ghostly legends. Notable tales include Railroad Bill (an outlaw folk hero), the Alabama White Thang (a hairy beast), Dead Children’s Playground (a famously haunted Huntsville cemetery), and the Boyington Oak in Mobile, which grew from the grave of an wrongfully executed man. [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] Top Alabama Legends and Lore Railroad Bill: An African American outlaw in the late 19th century who terrorized the L&N Railroad in Atmore, Alabama. He was a Robin Hood figure who stole goods and gave them to the poor before being killed in 1896. [ 1 ] The White Thang: A legendary, apox -like cryptid said to roam the rural woods of northern Alabama and the rural areas near Evergreen (known as the Bigfoot Capital of the state). It is described as a tall, white, hairy creature with glowing red eyes. [ 1 ] The Boyington Oak: In Mobile, Charles Boyington was executed for murder in 1834. He proclaimed his innocence and insisted an oak tree would grow on his grave as proof. Today, a massive oak tree stands directly over his resting spot in the Potter's Field section of Church Street Graveyard. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] Dead Children's Playground: Located just outside Huntsville's historic Maple Hill Cemetery, this playground is rumored to be where the spirits of departed children come to play at night, with locals often reporting swings moving on their own. [ 1 , 2 ] Atipa-Tcoba (Big Man-Eater): Rooted in deep Indigenous lore, this is a giant, cannibalistic monster from Muskogean and Creek (Alabama) traditions. The legends often describe it as an elephant-like giant, potentially tied to ancient mammoth fossils discovered in the region. [ 1 ]

title: Pennsylvania Lore
originalText: The Pennsylvania Dutch heavily influenced local folklore, blending European fairy tales with the rugged Appalachian landscape. Belief in "powwowing" (a form of faith healing and folk magic) was once widespread. Hex Signs: These geometric patterns painted on barns are deeply rooted in folklore as symbols meant to bring good fortune, ward off evil spirits, and protect livestock. The Squonk: Hailing from the hemlock forests of northern Pennsylvania, this famously ugly creature is so ashamed of its appearance that it hides and weeps constantly. If cornered by a hunter, the Squonk will dissolve entirely into a pool of tears and bubbles. Ghosts, Monsters, and Urban Legends The state's long industrial history and deep forests have given rise to various cryptids, spirits, and urban legends: The Green Man (Raymond Robinson): Based out of the South Park area near Pittsburgh. Robinson was severely disfigured by an electrical accident as a child and took to walking the roads at night. He became a celebrated local legend, with generations of Pittsburghers searching for "The Green Man" into the 1950s and beyond. Raystown Ray: Pennsylvania's own lake monster, said to lurk in the depths of Raystown Lake, with sightings stretching back decades. The Easton Monk: A notoriously dark tale from Easton tells of a greedy, corrupt monk who was hanged for beating an elderly woman to death, only for his body to spring back to life as a monstrous ghoul. The Kecksburg UFO (1965) In December 1965, a massive fireball streaked across the sky, crashing into the woods of Kecksburg, PA. Military cordons quickly locked down the area, sparking decades of folklore surrounding a crashed Soviet satellite or an alien spacecraft bearing Egyptian-like hieroglyphics on its hull.

title: Michigan Lore
originalText: The Michigan Dogman First reported in Wexford County in 1887, the Dogman is described as a 7-foot-tall, bipedal canine with the torso of a man and a piercing human scream. According to local legend, this fearsome beast emerges from the woods of the northern Lower Peninsula every 10 years during years ending in a 7. The Nain Rouge of Detroit Known as the "Demon of the Strait," the Nain Rouge (Red Dwarf) is a small, glowing-eyed creature whose appearance supposedly forewarns Detroit of impending disasters. According to local legends, the creature was spotted before the 1763 Battle of Bloody Run, the 1805 fire, and the 1967 riots. Today, Detroiters celebrate the annual Marche du Nain Rouge to chase the creature away and usher in a prosperous spring. Mishipeshu (The Great Lynx) Deeply embedded in the folklore of Great Lakes Native American tribes, Mishipeshu is a supernatural water panther with scales, serpent-like qualities, and sharp horns. Said to guard the rich copper deposits in Lake Superior, this powerful spirit is believed to create whirlpools, violent storms, and treacherous waters to protect its domain from intruders. Maritime Mysteries With thousands of shipwrecks scattered across the Great Lakes, Michigan has no shortage of nautical lore. The 1679 disappearance of Le Griffon —the first European vessel to sail the upper Great Lakes—is famous in the region, with some attributing its loss to a Native American prophet's curse.

title: Oklahoma Lore
originalText: Cryptids & Mythical Beings Deer Woman: A prominent figure in many Native American traditions (including Cherokee and Choctaw lore), she appears as a beautiful woman but has the hooves of a deer. She is often seen as a warning to young men who are disrespectful, wandering the woods to lure them away. Little People: Deeply rooted in indigenous folklore, these small, mischievous beings are said to reside in the woods and near rivers. In some traditions, their presence is indicated by blue "fairy lights." It is considered bad luck to speak their names or cut down trees where they live. The Oklahoma Dog Man: A cryptid described as having a muscular, athletic body covered in dark fur, but with the head of a hound. Numerous eyewitness accounts claim this creature chases cars on desolate highways, specifically keeping pace to terrify the driver rather than inflict harm. Haunted Places & Urban Legends Crybaby Bridges: Like many rural areas, Oklahoma has dozens of "Crybaby Bridges" (such as the Bobby Creek bridge). The legends usually claim a tragic tale of a mother and her infant, with local lore warning that if you stop your car and turn off your headlights, you can hear a baby crying. The Tulsa Hex House: A notorious real-estate legend from the 1940s involving a fraudulent medium and bizarre household abuse. The house was long rumored to emit negative energy, becoming a staple of Oklahoma ghost-lore. The Purple Church: Located in Spencer, this abandoned, vandalized church has long been the subject of local occult legends, with stories of demonic rituals and intense paranormal activity. Historical & Natural Mysteries The Anubis Caves: A series of shallow sandstone alcoves containing mysterious, ancient rock carvings that do not match the style of local tribes. Some have debated if the carvings represent ancient Egyptian, Celtic, or Phoenician visitors. The Hornet Spooklight : A legendary, glowing ball of light that appears on a rural back road straddling the Oklahoma-Missouri border. It has been reported since the late 19th century, bouncing and darting through the dark trees with no scientific consensus on what causes it. Frontier Tall Tales Weather Exaggeration: Oklahoma's intense, unpredictable weather is the subject of many folk stories. One famous tall tale features winds so strong that they "break your crowbar", and temperatures dropping so fast that frogs are frozen mid-leap with their heads still sticking out of the ice. The Cherokee Rose: A legend that tells of the Cherokee women shedding tears during the tragic Trail of Tears . The elders told them to look back, and where their tears fell, the Cherokee Rose—a flower with seven leaves representing the seven clans—began to bloom to give the people hope.

title: California Lore
originalText: The Dark Watchers (Big Sur) Dating back to Spanish colonial times and noted by Indigenous communities, these mysterious, towering (7 to 10 feet tall) shadowy figures are seen in the late afternoon standing on mountain ridges silently observing travelers. Lake Monsters and Cryptids Tahoe Tessie: California’s version of the Loch Ness monster, Tessie is said to be a 30- to 60-foot serpentine creature living in the deep, underwater caves of Lake Tahoe. Elsie of Lake Elsinore: A scaled, long-necked beast that locals and Indigenous observers claim roams the waters of this Southern California lake. Fresno Nightcrawler: Described as a bizarre, cartoonish pair of white, wide-leg pants with no torso, this stumbling cryptid was famously captured on security cameras in 2007 in Fresno and later in Yosemite.

title: Florida Lore
originalText: Florida’s folklore blends Native American myths, Spanish colonial legends, and Southern pioneer tales. Famous lore includes the Skunk Ape (Florida’s swamp-dwelling Bigfoot), the paranormal mysteries of Cassadaga (Florida's psychic capital), and the phantom cars rolling uphill on Lake Wales' Spook Hill . Florida boasts a distinct regional mythology shaped by its massive swamps, diverse cultural influences, and isolated pioneer settlements. The legends often reflect the wild, untamed nature of the peninsula: The Skunk Ape: The South’s version of Bigfoot. This large, hairy, foul-smelling cryptid is said to inhabit the remote wetland forests of the Everglades and Big Cypress. Sightings date back decades, with many locals claiming to have encountered the bipedal beast. Spook Hill (Lake Wales): One of Florida's oldest magnetic hill illusions. Folklore claims that a Native American chief and a giant alligator clashed on the hill long ago. Today, drivers put their cars in neutral and swear an unseen supernatural force pushes their vehicles uphill. Cassadaga Spiritualist Camp: Founded in 1894, this small town in Volusia County is renowned as the "Psychic Capital of the World". Its folklore is filled with tales of séances, Victorian-era spirits, and the infamous "Devil's Chair"—a brick bench where it is said the devil himself appears at midnight. The Fountain of Youth: The most enduring historical legend, tied to Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de León’s 1513 expedition. While Ponce de León never actually sought out an age-reversing spring in his journals, the myth remains deeply ingrained in St. Augustine's identity and Florida’s broader lore. The St. Johns River Monster ("Johnnie"): Florida's very own Loch Ness Monster. For generations, residents along the St. Johns River and in nearby Jacksonville have reported seeing a massive, horned serpentine beast or a "shrimp-colored" sea serpent. The Ghost Village (Everglades): Deep in the Everglades lies "The Lost City," an abandoned three-acre site wrapped in tall tales of hidden Confederate gold, Prohibition moonshine, and use by Al Capone.

title: Washington Lore
originalText: Indigenous Mythology & Landscapes Mt. Rainier and Mt. Adams: Known as Tahoma (or Tacoma), Mt. Rainier was often viewed as a sacred, towering, and volatile home to powerful spirits, with its eruptions and avalanches explained as spirit battles. Coyote Stories: Coyote is the central figure of Pacific Northwest trickster lore. Stories from the Klickitat, Nez Perce, and Chinook people detail how Coyote stole fire, shaped the course of the Columbia River, and defeated the monster beaver, Wishpoosh, at Lake Cle Elum. Cryptids & Monsters Sasquatch (Bigfoot): Washington records more Bigfoot sightings than any other state. The lore spans from Indigenous oral traditions to modern-day sightings near Mount Rainier, Snoqualmie Pass, and Skamania County. The Lake Chelan Dragon ( N’hah’hahat’q ): Indigenous cultures share legends of a long, scaly, alligator-like monster hiding in the deep underwater cave systems of Lake Chelan. Settler stories later claimed the beast hatched from a Scottish pirate's egg in 1812. Batsquatch: A lesser-known winged cryptid with leathery wings and glowing red eyes, said to inhabit remote volcanic mountains like Mount St. Helens. Caddy (Cadborosaurus): A sea monster spotted off the Washington and British Columbia coast, described as having a long neck and the head of a horse. Modern Legends & Tall Tales The Pacific Northwest Tree Octopus: A famous internet-era tall tale and urban legend stating this cephalopod lives in the rainforests of the Olympic Peninsula, using its tentacles to camouflage in the trees. Ape Cave Lava Tubes: Located near Mount St. Helens, these caves get their name from a 1920s local lore that an ape-like monster inhabited them

title: Indiana Lore
originalText: Indiana folklore is a rich tapestry of Native American legends, midwestern tall tales, and chilling urban legends , f rom the ghostly shores of Lake Michigan to the dense, rural woo ds. Haunted Places & Local Legends Diana of the Dunes (Indiana Dunes State Park): A popular legend on the shores of Lake Michigan describes a mysterious, ethereal woman roaming the beach and running into the lake. The legend is inspired by the real-life Alice Mabel Gray, a brilliant socialite who abandoned Chicago in 1915 to live as a hermit in the dunes. 100 Step Cemetery (Brazil): Located in Clay County, this cemetery features a crumbling staircase. Urban legends warn that if you climb and count the steps at midnight, the number will change on the way back down, or you will see a vision of your own death from the old caretaker. House of Blue Lights (Indianapolis): Once located in the northeast side of Indianapolis, this sprawling estate belonged to eccentric millionaire Skiles Test. Throughout the 20th century, locals told stories of the property being endlessly decorated in strange, glowing blue Christmas lights, sparking rumors of hauntings and secret cults. Cryptids & Monsters Beast of Busco (Churubusco): In 1949, a local farmer claimed to see a colossal, boat-sized snapping turtle in Fulk Lake. Dubbed "Oscar," the turtle caused a media frenzy with locals attempting to drain the lake and trap the beast. Churubusco still celebrates its legendary turtle today with an annual "Turtle Days" festival. Crawfordsville Monster: In 1891, terrified residents reported a floating, headless, glowing creature flapping through the night sky. While it caused mass panic at the time, many historians and investigators later attributed the sightings to a frightened, migrating flock of killdeer. The Ohio River Monster: Originating in 1955 near Evansville, locals reported a human-sized, green-skinned creature with hairy arms and claws lurking in the waters, allegedly attempting to pull swimmers under. Native American Lore & Giants Legends of the Wabash Valley: Early Native American tribes, like the Piankashaw and Miami, shared stories of Paissa (forest trickster spirits) and massive giants that roamed the dark woodlands across the Ohio River. Lake Manitou (Rochester): The Potawatomi referred to this body of water as "Lake Man- i -toe" (the Devil's Lake). Legends stated the lake was nearly bottomless and harbored an evil spirit, forcing tribesmen to avoid fishing or canoeing on its waters. [

title: Wyoming Lore
originalText: Native American Legends Devils Tower: According to the oral traditions of the Arapaho, Cheyenne, and Sioux tribes, the spectacular rock formation was created to save seven young girls from a giant bear. As the bear chased them, the girls climbed a low rock and prayed to the Great Spirit. The rock rose high into the sky, and the bear clawed the sides, creating the vertical striations we see today. The Nimerigar (Little People): Shoshone and Crow folklore tells of the Nimerigar , a race of hostile, pygmy-like people who lived in the Pedro Mountains. In 1932, a mummified body of a tiny human was discovered in the region, fueling speculation that these tales were based on a real, ancient species of humans. Water Babies: According to Shoshone tradition, these childlike spiritual beings dwell in the rivers and lakes of the Wind River region. They are said to lure people to the water by mimicking the cries of infants. Wild West & Pioneer Tall Tales Jim Bridger’s Tall Tales: Famed mountain man and scout Jim Bridger is legendary for his tall tales. He famously told stories of a "petrified forest" where petrified birds sang petrified songs, and a river that ran so fast over rocks that it generated friction and boiled the water . The Headless Bride: A popular ghost story tracing back to an old Cheyenne boarding house. The bride was murdered on her wedding night, and it is said her spirit wanders the historic buildings searching for her lost head. The Ship of Death: A legendary ghost ship that supposedly haunts the North Platte River. Appearing out of a thick, ominous mist, it is crewed by frosted phantoms who are said to gather and reveal the identity of loved ones who will die that day. Cryptids & Natural Mysteries Lake Desmet Monster: Named after Father Pierre Jean De Smet, this large, serpentine creature is said to inhabit Lake De Smet in Sheridan County. Early Native Americans and settlers alike claimed to see it, and locals noted horses would become highly uncontrollable near the water. The Vedauwoo Monster: Nestled in the Laramie Mountains, the Vedauwoo recreation area is named after the Arapaho word for "earthborn spirits". Local lore speaks of a shapeshifting monster that lures unsuspecting campers by mimicking the sound of an owl calling out in the night.

title: Utah Lore
originalText: Cryptozoology & Monsters Bear Lake Monster: A serpentine, 50-foot creature with legs and a cow-like head. The first reports originated in the 1860s in the border town of Garden City. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] Skinwalker: Rooted in Navajo tradition, Skinwalkers are malevolent, shape-shifting witches capable of taking the form of animals. Sightings are deeply feared in the Uintah Basin and around the Four Corners area. [ 1 , 2 ] Utah Lake Water Babies: In Ute and Great Basin Native folklore, these are small, spiritual humanoids believed to inhabit Utah Lake, sometimes said to lure people into the water. Haunted Locations & Cures Allen Park Once owned by a local eccentric, the site is populated by peacocks and rustic cottages. Local legend dubbed it " Hobbitville ," claiming it was inhabited by a community of little people. Dead Horse Point A dramatic overlook with a legend of a ghostly, wild white horse said to haunt the precipice after the tragic death of a herd. Lost Treasures & Historical Myths Montezuma’s Treasure: A legend claiming immense Aztec gold was smuggled into Utah's Red Rock country. Generations of prospectors have dug through the canyons near Kanab, convinced it is protected by ancient booby traps. The Dream Mine: An ongoing, century-old prophecy involving a gold mine in Salem, Utah, famously dug by locals acting upon a dream of John H. Koyle, who prophesied it would save people during an upcoming economic collapse. Native American Legends & The Great Basin Fremont and Ute Rock Art: The deep, mysterious pictographs and petroglyphs carved into canyon walls across the state, such as those at Nine Mile Canyon, represent ancient religious spirits and hunting chronicles that folklorists continue to study. Gadianton Robbers: A band of secret, shadowy individuals mentioned in the Book of Mormon, often woven into local folklore as supposedly roaming and hiding out in the Wasatch Mountains.

title: Idaho Lore
originalText: Idaho folklore blends deep Indigenous oral traditions with rowdy pioneer tales of the frontier, mining booms, and the untamed wilderness. It is rich with cryptids like the "Sharlie" lake monster in McCall, cannibal dwarves in the Owyhee Mountains, the sorrowful Water Babies, and humorous tall tales of jackalopes. Wilderness Cryptids & Spirits Sharlie (The Payette Lake Monster) Residing in the deep, icy waters of Payette Lake in McCall, Sharlie is Idaho’s most famous lake monster. First reported by loggers and Indigenous tribes in the early 1920s, the creature is frequently described as a 35-to-60-foot serpent with multiple humps. Sightings skyrocketed in the 1940s, and today, she serves as more of a beloved local mascot than a fearful beast. The Bear Lake Monster Straddling the Idaho-Utah border, Bear Lake is the supposed home of an aquatic cryptid dating back to the 1800s. Originally featured in early Mormon pioneer accounts, the monster was described as serpent-like, swimming incredibly fast, and occasionally snatching people from the water's edge. The Owyhee Cannibal Dwarves According to local Indigenous (Shoshone) legends, tiny, twisted creatures only a couple of feet tall once roamed the Owyhee Mountains. Known as the Nimarigar, these beings were said to have long tails, sharp teeth, and a penchant for eating children and unsuspecting travelers. Tragedy & The Supernatural Water Babies of the Bear River Perhaps one of the most haunting and tragic pieces of Idaho folklore centers on the Great Basin tribes' tales of Water Babies. The legend tells of a time of severe starvation, during which some mothers sorrowfully placed their babies in the river to spare them a lifetime of hardship. According to the oral tradition, the spirits of these children never left the water. Campers near the river and the Great Salt Lake often report hearing the faint sounds of crying or giggling on quiet, breezy nights. Frontier & Mining Lore The Legend of the Iron Door One of Idaho’s most famous lost treasure myths takes place in the steep mountains near Malad City. According to the tale, a group of bandits who robbed a bank in the 1800s hauled a heavy, iron bank vault door into a remote mountain cave in southeastern Idaho to hide their loot. Prospectors claim the door has been located over the decades, but it either cannot be opened or the cave disappears when they leave to fetch heavy tools. Jackalopes and Snipe Hunts Like much of the American West, Idaho has its fair share of playful tall tales used to prank newcomers. The Jackalope: A legendary cross between a jackrabbit and an antelope. The Snipe Hunt: A classic rural prank where eager newcomers are given a burlap sack and told to stand in a pitch-black field in the Idaho wilderness to wait for "snipes" to be driven toward them by the rest of the group.
