Mélusine (Poitou): A beautiful water spirit who transforms into a half-serpent every Saturday. She married a lord on the condition he never spy on her, leading to tragedy when he broke his promise. The Questing Beast (Arthurian): A creature with the head of a serpent, the body of a leopard, the buttocks of a lion, and the feet of a har e . The Cheval Gauvin (Jura Mountains): A malevolent, demonic water horse that tries to lure riders to their doom. Ankou (Brittany): The personification of death. Often depicted as a tall, gaunt man wearing a wide hat and long cloak, he drives a squeaking, skeletal cart to collect the souls of the deceased. Dames Blanches (White Ladies): Female spirits and spectral fairies found across Normandy and the Pyrenees. They act as guardians of bridges and natural phenomena but will curse travelers who ignore or anger them. Much of French lore overlaps with Celtic mythology, heavily localized in the Forest of Brocéliande (modern-day Paimpont) . Merlin & Viviane: It is here that Merlin was famously trapped in an invisible prison by the Lady of the Lake. The Fountain of Barenton: A legendary enchanted spring where pouring water onto a specific rock is said to summon violent storms. Charles Perrault: In the 17th century, he compiled foundational stories like Cinderella , Little Red Riding Hood , Sleeping Beauty , and Puss in Boots . The Song of Roland ( La Chanson de Roland ): France's oldest surviving major work of literature. It tracks the semi-mythical, heroic last stand of Charlemagne’s knight, Roland, in the Pyrenees and the magic of his unbreakable sword, Durandal.

title: Kyrgyzstan Lore
originalText: The Epic of Manas : The cornerstone of Kyrgyz identity and the longest epic poem in the world. It chronicles the legendary warrior Manas and his descendants ( Semetey and Seytek ) who unite the forty Kyrgyz tribes against foreign invaders. Er Töshtük : A mythical epic where the hero descends into the underworld to rescue his loved ones, battling monsters and dark spirits. Mother Deer (Bugu Tribe) : The legend of the Bugu tribe tells the story of a mother deer who saved two children, becoming the sacred ancestor of the tribe. Kumayyk : Mythological stories about a magical hunting dog possessing supernatural powers that often aid the heroes in epics. Lake Issyk-Kul Legend holds that a beautiful girl was imprisoned by a ruthless Khan, but preferred to throw herself from a dungeon window rather than be captured. The clear mountain water rushed in to flood his palace, forming the salty, ice-free lake. Jeti-Oguz (Seven Bulls) A legend explaining a dramatic red rock formation, created when a Khan's stolen wife was given a magical potion that turned the seven bulls pursuing her into stone. A local legend states a Khan locked his daughter in this tower because a fortune teller warned she would die from a spider bite. Despite his precautions, a poisonous spider hid in a basket of grapes and took her life. The Evil Eye : Grandmothers traditionally tie red threads on babies' wrists and burn archal (juniper) in the yurt to ward off misfortune. Taboos : Common folklore superstitions include that spilling milk brings bad luck, cutting nails at night shortens one's life, and pointing at the stars causes one's fingers to rot. Musical Storytelling : Traditional oral folklore is accompanied by instruments like the komuz (a three-stringed lute). The Woman in Red : A popular local spirit is said to appear on the night roads near Lake Issyk-Kul, acting as an omen or spirit warning drivers of danger.

title: Congo-brazzaville Lore
originalText: At the heart of Bakongo cosmology is Nzambi Mpungu , the supreme creator and ruler of the earth and the heavens. Nzazi: The god of thunder who commands a pack of lightning dogs. Mbumba: The rainbow serpent who controls the waters and often conflicts with Nzazi for control of the world. Simbis: Revered nature spirits who guard the rivers, forests, and local ecosystems. Mokele-mbembe: A legendary, semi-aquatic monster—often described as dinosaur-like—said to inhabit the deep river systems like Lake Télé. Biloko: Cannibalistic trolls or dwarves from local mythology known to lure travelers deep into the jungle. Indombe: A colossal, mythological copper snake several miles long, said to live in the canopy of the forest. The Tortoise frequently appears as the ultimate trickster hero, using cleverness and wit to outsmart much larger, stronger animals like the Elephant and Hippopotamus. Tales often explore themes of jealousy, humility, twin brothers, and magical elements like the Magic Tree that imprisons and frees villagers along the river. Nkisi: Central to Congolese spirituality are Nkisi —sacred objects, often carved wooden figures, that contain spiritual forces or medicines to heal the sick, offer protection, and govern social laws. Preservation: Modern projects like the Odzala-Kokoua National Park-based initiatives have actively gathered traditional myths and paired them with modern visual storytelling to keep these oral narratives alive today.

title: Iraq Lore
originalText: Iraqi folklore is deeply rooted in ancient Sumerian, Akkadian, and Babylonian traditions. These early myths established themes that resonate throughout regional storytelling today. The Epic of Gilgamesh: Perhaps the world’s oldest written story, it recounts the adventures of the King of Uruk as he searches for immortality. The Descent of Inanna: This myth recounts how the goddess Inanna travels through the seven gates of the underworld to visit her sister Ereshkigal, setting the stage for folklore based on underworld journeys. Atra-Hasis & Enuma Elish: Foundational creation myths where gods clash, create humanity out of clay, and send a great flood to reduce human population. Iraqi folklore is perhaps best known internationally for its connections to Baghdad, the historical hub of the Abbasid Caliphate. The One Thousand and One Nights (Alf Layla wa -Layla): Put together in Iraq, this massive collection features stories told by Scheherazade. It is the origin of legendary characters like Sinbad the Sailor , Ali Baba , and tales of Aladdin . The Tanabilah : A classic Baghdadi folk story about the first documented elder care home, which featured sheltered beds, gardens, and 3 meals a day for elders without support. The Tantal: A menacing, shape-shifting spirit in Iraqi lore. Often living near water, it can shower a person with wealth or pull them to a watery grave. Folktales from Iraq: Collections, such as those compiled by C.G. Campbell in southern Iraq, focus on quick-witted heroes, sultans, fishermen, and magical happenings. Northern Iraq Folklore: A diverse blend featuring Aramaic-speaking Syriac Christians and Kurdish Muslims, highlighting fables of animals (like the dog, ewe, and wolf) and stories of resilience. Mājīnā : A popular Iraqi folkloric tradition that acts as a "trick-or-treat" style custom, where children go door-to-door in neighborhoods to sing traditional songs and receive treats. Superstitions: It is widely considered good luck if a stork builds a nest on your home's roof. Conversely, people with blue eyes or those who have had no children were historically kept away from birth celebrations to prevent harm to the baby.

title: Hungarian Lore
originalText: Central to ancient Hungarian belief is the Táltos , a person born with extra teeth or bones who possesses supernatural healing, the ability to read minds, and the power to project their soul into the spirit realm ( révülés ). Another central pillar is the Turul bird, a giant raptor that appeared in a dream to Emese, prophesying that her descendants would become kings. Other notable creatures include: Garabonciás : A wandering wizard who commands storms and rides dragons ( Sárkány ). Szépasszony : The "beautiful lady" who dances in storms and lures young men away. Mumus : The Hungarian equivalent of the boogeyman, used to frighten misbehaving children. Hétmérföldes csizma : Seven-league boots used to cross the flat plains ( Alföld ) in a single step. Tűzmadár : The firebird, which brings light, magic, and healing feathers. Bűvös malom : A magical mill that continuously grinds out food, wealth, or even salt.

title: Malaysia Lore
originalText: Puteri Gunung Ledang (Johor): The legendary fairy princess of Mount Ophir who demanded impossible tasks (like a bridge of gold or a bowl of an infant's blood) from the Sultan of Malacca to win her hand. Mahsuri (Langkawi): A tragic 19th-century tale of a falsely accused woman whose execution released white blood, causing her to curse the island with seven generations of drought and misfortune. Hang Tuah (Malacca): The ultimate Malay folk hero and warrior, whose unyielding loyalty to the Sultan serves as the pinnacle of bravery and silat martial arts. Batu Belah Batu Bertangkup (Selangor): A cautionary tale of a neglected, grieving mother who was swallowed whole by a magical, devouring rock after her children ate her favorite fish. Sang Kancil: The clever mouse-deer who outwits larger predators (like crocodiles and tigers) in fables. Pontianak: The most infamous ghost in Malay lore; she is a vengeful spirit of a woman who died during childbirth, recognizable by her long black hair and the scent of jasmine. Penanggalan : A terrifying vampire-like spirit consisting of a disembodied female head with its internal organs dangling below, flying through the night to hunt for blood. Toyol : A ghostly, green-skinned infant spirit conjured by a shaman using black magic to perform mischief or steal money for its master. Orang Bunian : Mythical "invisible people" who dwell deep within dense Malaysian forests, often said to lure lost travelers into their hidden, magical realm. Bujang Senang (Sarawak): The terrifying legend of a massive, man-eating crocodile that roamed the Batang Lupar river before its capture. Mount Kinabalu (Sabah): A Kadazan-Dusun legend tells of an angry dragon holding a giant pearl at the peak, while another folklore recounts a Chinese prince who scaled the mountain to find the creature.

title: Cameroon Lore
originalText: The Miengu (Singular: Jengu): Celebrated water spirits in the traditional beliefs of the coastal Sawa people. Often described as beautiful mermaid-like figures with long hair and gap-toothed smiles, they are believed to act as intermediaries between the spiritual and human worlds. [ 1 , 2 ] Efasa Moto: The formidable mountain god of the Bakweri people near Mount Cameroon. He is believed to be half-human, half-stone, and his anger causes natural disasters. The Ebigane: A fearsome monster from the Fang legends (Mvett) that can shape-shift between human and animal forms—often described as a terrifying cross between a bat, a buffalo, and a vampire. Creation Myths: Stories vary by region, such as the Bakundu creation myth, which explores the origin of both good and evil races on Earth, and the Great Spirit Gba-Só worshiped by the Gbaya people in the East. The Tortoise: In the coastal regions (Duala/Batanga), the tortoise is revered in folklore as a clever genius. Conversely, savannah tribes like the Bafia view the tortoise as an ominous bringer of trouble. Trickster and Orphan Tales: Common moral allegories, such as the Sense-Pass-King trope or orphan heroines, center on outsmarting the proud and punishing jealousy, pride, and gluttony.

title: Sicilian Lore
originalText: Colapesce : A young fisherman from Messina named Nicola who loved the sea so much he tested his limits underwater, eventually staying below to hold up one of Sicily's three structural pillars to keep the island from sinking. The Moor’s Heads ( Teste di Moro ): Colorful ceramic vases shaped like human faces originating from a grim folktale about a young Sicilian noblewoman who decapitated her foreign lover and used his head as a basil planter. Mount Etna Giants: Greek lore says the monster Typhon or the giant Enceladus is trapped beneath Mount Etna, causing eruptions and rumblings whenever they turn or breathe fire. Aci and Galatea: A coastal myth explaining the origins of towns near Etna, where a jealous cyclops named Polyphemus killed the shepherd Aci, who was then transformed into a flowing river by the gods. Opera dei Pupi (Sicilian Puppet Theater): Traditional marionette theater dramatizing medieval knight battles, the crusades, and the epic poems of Charlemagne. The Trinacria : The official symbol of Sicily featuring a three-legged Medusa head, representing the island's three geographic capes and ancient protective magic. Truvature : Folk beliefs regarding hidden, spell-guarded treasures scattered across the rural Sicilian landscape and caves.

title: Guatemalan Lore
originalText: La Llorona: "The Weeping Woman" is a tragic spirit doomed to wander rivers and bodies of water at night, endlessly weeping and searching for the children she drowned. El Sombrerón : A tiny, mysterious man dressed in black with a huge hat and heeled boots. He rides into farms to braid the manes of horses and enchants young women with his beautiful singing voice, eventually causing them to die of infatuation. La Siguanaba : A beautiful seductress who haunts ravines and isolated rivers. She lures wandering, unfaithful men deep into the wilderness before turning around to reveal a horrifying horse-like or skull face. Deeply rooted in indigenous communities (especially around Lake Atitlán), ancient traditions and shapeshifting tales are still actively practiced and spoken about . Los Nahuales : Belief that every human has an animal counterpart, spirit, or totem. Shamans (or curanderos ) frequently communicate with a person's nahual to heal illnesses or solve mysteries. El Cadejo : Two supernatural dogs that roam the night. A benign white dog protects women and children, while a malevolent black dog watches over drunks, keeping them safe on their walk home but leading them down a dark path. Los Aluxes : Mischievous, invisible forest dwarfs who are guardians of the land. Farmers often build small houses for them in exchange for protecting their crops. Maximon (or San Simón): A famous and controversial folk saint worshiped heavily in Santiago Atitlán. He represents a syncretism of Maya gods, Spanish conquerors, and Catholic saints. Devotees offer him cigars, alcohol, and money in exchange for protection, good luck, and love.

title: Eritrea Lore
originalText: Eritrean mythology is populated by a rich variety of spirits, fairies, and omens passed down by elders: Deki Hidrtna: Benevolent female fairies or woodland spirits said to reside in rivers, canyons, and deep forests. They are known to play music, share food, and occasionally guide humans. Buda: The pervasive belief in the "evil eye". In traditional folklore, this power is often associated with metalworkers or those from different social groups, and it is warded off through specific blessings and rituals. Zar Spirits: Unseen, spiritual entities that can interact with or possess humans, which are treated through traditional healing customs and holy water ceremonies. Storytelling traditionally takes place around a fire to pass on wisdom and cultural values. Common tales include: Trickster Tales: Tales featuring clever figures like Abunawas (a coastal trickster), whose stories are used to teach lessons about clever justice, wit, and fairness over rigid rule following. Animal Fables: Stories featuring hyenas, leopards, and foxes are used to pass down life lessons. For example, fables about leopards attacking weaker prey serve as metaphors for the cycle of revenge and the need for careful observation. Everyday life and social customs are heavily guided by inherited beliefs: The Coffee Ceremony: A deeply ingrained social and spiritual ritual. The burning of incense rocks during this ceremony acts as a physical and spiritual method to repel bad spirits. Counting Households: Traditional village elders often avoid counting the exact number of members in their household. It is superstitiously believed that if the devil learns the exact count, he might reduce the number. Wedding Traditions: Dancing is viewed as a language of emotion. Guests show appreciation and offer financial support to the newlyweds by sticking money to the foreheads or shirts of dancers.

title: Palestine State Lore
originalText: The Hikaye Tradition Definition : Fictitious oral tales traditionally told by women over age 70. Setting : Spontaneously narrated during winter evenings at home among small groups of women and children. Purpose : Offers a subtle critique of Middle Eastern Arab society and family structures from a female perspective. Tunjur , Tunjur : A well-known cumulative folk story about a tiny clay pot that comes to life and goes on a journey. The Daughter of the Rose and the Jasmine : A distinct regional variant of the Cinderella narrative. Collections : Major academic and cultural preservation works like [ Speak, Bird, Speak Again ] (by Ibrahim Muhawi and Sharif Kanaana) document dozens of authentic rural tales divided into cycles of family, courtship, and quests. Deep Roots : Customs and agricultural calendars merge ancient Near Eastern and Canaanite seasonal rhythms with later monotheistic traditions. Symbolism : The olive tree acts as an enduring motif representing peace, heritage, and connection to the land across millennia.

title: Zambia Lore
originalText: Kalulu the Hare: The most famous clever trickster in Zambian and Bantu folklore (known in Tumbuka and Bemba traditions) who outsmarts powerful beasts like the lion and elephant using wit. Fulu the Tortoise: Regarded as the wisest and most grounded animal, sometimes the only one who can match or check Kalulu's schemes. Chimbwi the Hyena: Frequently cast as the greedy, foolish villain who falls for Kalulu's traps. Leza / Lesa / Nyambe: The Supreme Creator and sky god, recognized under varying names across different linguistic groups like the Tonga, Bemba, and Lozi. The Sky Is So High: An early belief stating the sky used to hang low like a mosquito net, allowing people to talk directly to God before human behavior pushed it upward. Nyami Nyami : The sacred river god of the Tonga people, depicted as a dragon-like serpent with a fish head residing in the Zambezi River near the Kariba Dam. Ilomba and Ikisonga : Mythical familiars and monster-slayers tied to traditional bush and river superstitions.

title: Paraguay Lore
originalText: According to Guaraní creation myth, the union of the spirit Tau and the mortal Keraná produced seven legendary, cursed brothers who shape Paraguayan folklore: Teju Jagua: A lizard with a dog's head, known as the lord of caverns and fruits. Mbói Tu'í: A giant snake with a parrot's head, protector of amphibians and moisture. Moñái : A horned snake and thief of field animals, tied to open fields and air. Jasy Jatere : A golden-haired, wand-carrying elf who wanders at noon to charm and lead children away. Kurupi: A fast, wild dwarf representing fertility and sexuality who guards the deep woods. Ao Ao : A ferocious, sheep- or boar-like creature that hunts humans in packs, shouting its own name. Luisón ( Luison ): The seventh son—a terrifying man-beast or werewolf-like entity that roams cemeteries at night eating the dead. El Pombero : A famous nocturnal goblin of the forest. He whistles in the dark, protects wildlife, can bring good or bad luck to farmers, and punishes those who disrespect nature.

title: Slovenia Lore
originalText: Kurent (Korant): The most famous traditional mascot of Slovenian folklore, a chaotic and joyful pagan spirit clad in sheepskins and cowbells meant to chase away winter. [ 1 , 2 ] Martin Krpan: A folksy, ultra-strong fictional giant-slayer from an inner Carniolan village who traded contraband English salt and saved the Viennese court from a brute. King Matjaž: A mythical, sleeping good king of Carantania who waits inside a mountain with his army until his beard grows around a stone table nine times. Kekec: A brave, clever fictional shepherd boy from the Slovenian mountains who outwits wicked peddlers and giants in regional children's stories. Zlatorog (Goldenhorn): A magical white alpine ibex/chamois living near Mount Triglav whose golden horns unlock a massive mountain treasure. Ajdi: A race of benevolent or fearsome pre-Christian giants said to have built the early settlements and tossed massive boulders across the alpine valleys. Žalik Žene / Bele Žene ("White Women"): Benevolent mountain fairies or nymphs who helped local shepherds, spun thread, and tended to flocks. Perkmandlc: A helpful or mischievous mining gnome living in deep shafts around towns like Trbovlje and Velenje, warning miners of danger. Ljubljana Dragon: The fierce protector of the capital city, whose statues now decorate the famous Dragon Bridge.

title: Qatar Lore
originalText: May and Ghilân : A foundational Al Khor legend about a boat race between a wealthy fleet owner ( Ghilân ) and a skilled female captain (May) that inspired the invention of the dhow boat sail. Bu Daryah (Lord of the Sea): A malevolent water spirit or jinni said to stalk pearl divers and sailors at night, causing psychological distress or pulling men into the dark depths. The Donkey Lady ( Homarat Al-Guyla ): A half-woman, half-donkey creature with hoofed feet used by parents during the midday heat to scare children from wandering outside during siesta time. Al Fisaikra : A magical porgy fish from a popular folktale that helps a mistreated young girl escape and find a better life. Al-Ardha: The traditional sword dance performed during national holidays, weddings, and the Qaffal ceremony welcoming back pearl divers. Oral Transmission: Traditionally shared in the majlis or around desert campfires, these dynamic stories have been modernly cataloged by projects like the Qatar Museums Hazawy Series.

title: Jiangsu Lore
originalText: Wu Cheng'en and Journey to the West : Born in Huai'an, the legendary Ming dynasty author Wu Cheng'en drew heavily from local river-town storytelling and regional myths to weave the epic tale of the Monkey King. [ 1 ] Madam White Snake (Baishe Zhuan): One of China's Four Great Folktales is deeply rooted in the Zhenjiang region. The tragic romance of Lady White Snake and Xu Xian features iconic local folklore locations like the Jinshan Temple. The Jiangshi (Hopping Ghosts): Deeply rooted in Taoist funerary traditions, the jiangshi (hopping ghost or Chinese vampire) is a staple of regional folklore. Traditionally, Taoist priests were believed to reanimate corpses, guiding them to hop along mountain roads so they could be buried in their hometowns. Baojuan (Precious Scrolls): In towns like Changshu, the recitation of prosimetric "Baojuan" texts remains a prevalent folklore tradition. These vernacular stories are chanted during communal temple festivals to honor tutelary local deities. Qiantong Boat Gathering: Held annually during the Qingming Festival in Jiangyan, this vibrant water activity sees hundreds of colorful wooden boats racing to drumbeats, celebrating the unity and courage of the northern Jiangsu water town people. Shan'ge (Mountain Songs): Traditional folk singing from southern Jiangsu's Wu-speaking region. Historically sung by farmers and boatmen, these tunes encompass labor songs, romantic ballads, and historical legends.

title: Henan Lore
originalText: The Yellow Emperor (Huangdi): Legend places the birthplace and capital of Huangdi, the mythical ancestor of the Chinese people, in Xinzheng , Henan. The Yellow River valley is where he is said to have united tribes and established the core tenets of Chinese civilization. The Kitchen God: The widely known Chinese legend of the Kitchen God (Zao Jun) and his wives originates from Henan folklore. The tale, which spans from heaven to hell, weaves traditional rural customs, marital loyalty, and divine judgment. Creation Myths: In nearby Huaiyang county, the mythological figures Nüwa (who created humanity) and Fuxi (who created the Eight Trigrams and fishing nets) are heavily revered, with ancient temples built in their honor. Shaolin Kung Fu: Centered in the Songshan Mountains of Dengfeng , Henan, the Shaolin Temple is the legendary birthplace of Zen Buddhism and Shaolin Kung Fu. Its folklore emphasizes both physical discipline and harmony with the universe. Tai Chi: The Chen Village ( Chenjiagou ) in Wen County, Henan, is the official birthplace of Tai Chi. The martial art’s folklore roots itself in observing the natural harmony of the Yin and Yang . Datiehua (Beating Iron Flowers): Originating in the Song Dynasty, this thrilling firework folk art was created by ancient metal craftsmen. Performers in heavy sheepskin coats throw ladles of molten iron into the night air against wooden planks, creating a spectacular shower of golden sparks. Dragon Boat Festival Roots: Deeply embedded in the Central Plains culture, Henan folklore champions the dragon as a central totem. The reverence for the dragon as a divine, weather-controlling creature is highly associated with the life-giving (and sometimes devastating) Yellow River. Zhuihu Ballads: Traditional Henan folk storytelling features the zhuizi —a narrative singing style accompanied by a bowed lute. The lyrical themes are heavily based on Taoist stories, ancient chants, and everyday life. Only Henan (Zhongyuan Drama): Modern-day Henan heavily preserves its own local stories and theatrical legacy. The massive immersive theatrical park "Only Henan" brings centuries of Central Plains history, folk beliefs, and ancient capital culture (such as Kaifeng and Luoyang) to life for millions of visitors.

title: Sichuan Lore
originalText: Mount Emei's White Snake : One of China’s most famous love stories is rooted in Sichuan's Mt. Emei. It follows a thousand-year-old white snake spirit ( Bai Suzhen ) and her green serpent companion ( Xiaoqing ) who take human form to experience the mortal world and find love in the face of a rigid Buddhist priest. Sun Wukong (The Monkey King) : While popularized in Journey to the West , regional Chuan Miao (River Miao) folklore features different variations of a monkey spirit that escorts emperors and tends to the Dragon King's injuries. The Jiuzhaigou Goddess : Tibetan folklore from northern Sichuan tells of a beautiful girl named Wonuo who was gifted golden bells by a goddess; her ringing bells brought crystal-clear creeks to the drought-ridden, barren mountains. Shan Xiao ( 山魈 ) : A one-legged mountain spirit (originally described in classical texts) that ancient Sichuan travelers believed caused fever and madness, scaring them into shouting loudly in mountain passes to drive spirits away. Jiangshi ( 殭屍 ) : The concept of the hopping vampire is deeply tied to regional Sichuan folklore, where early Daoist-influenced stories describe rigid corpses animated by terror or improper burial. Qiang Folk Religion : Deep in the mountains of Ngawa, traditional Qiang shamans known as duāngōng act as the custodians of local mythology. They perform complex rituals to mountain and sky gods, culminating in intense rites like the "sitting on top of the mountain". The Sichuan Massacre Myth : Historical folklore from the Ming-Qing transition centers around the rebel leader Zhang Xianzhong, with legends (partially spun as Qing dynasty propaganda) attributing the mass depopulation of the province to his supernatural wrath and bloody conquests. Sichuan Opera ( 川 剧 ) : Traditional lore comes alive through this regional art form, famous for bian lian (face-changing) and folk dramas like Pijin's Tumbling Lantern and The Story of Funu . Shadow Play : A disappearing art form historically prominent along promenades in Chengdu, depicting ancient folklore through intricate shadow puppets.

title: Fujian Lore
originalText: Mazu (Goddess of the Sea): The most iconic figure in Fujian mythology. Born on Meizhou Island, she is revered as the protector of fishermen and sailors. Her cult has spread globally from this coastal epicenter. [ 1 , 2 ] Sun Wukong (The Monkey King): Beyond the classic Journey to the West , Fujian houses numerous regional temples dedicated to the Monkey King, elevating him from a literary character to a formally worshipped folk deity. You Shen ( 游神 ): A centuries-old Daoist and local folk tradition where elaborate statues of deities are paraded through village streets to bring prosperity, health, and protection to the community. Hakka Tulou: The folklore of the Hakka people is embedded in their Tulou —massive, circular, fortified earthen buildings. These structures were built to foster community and protect the clan, inspiring legends of unity and resilience. Li Ji Slays the Great Serpent: A famous southern Chinese folktale (often associated with ancient Fujian) about a brave village girl who sacrifices herself to slay a giant, man-eating serpent, reflecting themes of courage and female empowerment. Liuyue Liu (The 6th of June Festival): A traditional celebration deeply tied to local legends, particularly observed by the She minority ethnic groups living in the mountainous regions of Fujian. Songbooks and Puppetry: Fujian is famous for " Dongshan Songbook" ( Dongshan Gece ) and shadow/glove puppetry, which have been used for centuries to pass down tragic, romantic, and heroic local sagas (such as tales of the region's ancient generals). Oral Histories of Women: Scholars have compiled collections of village folktales (such as Imagining Women: Fujian Folk Tales ) that reveal the everyday lives of common people, providing an alternative perspective to male-dominated Confucian lore.

title: Hunan Lore
originalText: 1. Sacred Mountains & The Fox Spirit Tianmen Mountain: Famous for the "Heaven's Gate" cave, it is heavily steeped in folklore regarding the legend of the Fox Lady . According to myth, local spirits inhabit the soaring peaks, and the mountain itself is considered a portal to the divine. Zhang Wulang: A major deity in the shamanistic Meishan culture of central Hunan. He is a wild, warrior-like spirit who is often depicted upside down. Locals view him as a patron of the hunt and a protector of the rugged mountain tribes. Hundun (Chaos): One of China's core primordial creation myths features the faceless, multi-winged being named Hundun , who symbolizes the swirling, chaotic mass before the creation of the universe. Miao Drum Dance: Originating in the Xiangxi region, this dance was supposedly invented by young villagers who stripped the skin off a crop-destroying beast to create drums. They beat the drums to scare away other beasts and spirits. Tujia Hand-Waving Dance: A centuries-old ritual focused on ancestor worship, blending dance, singing, and drama to commemorate historic tribal battles. Nüshu Script: The only known writing system developed exclusively by women, created in the remote counties of Jiangyong . Women used this secretive, phonetic script to write "third-day missives" (cloth-bound booklets of grief and well-wishes) passed down to newlywed friends. Flower Drum Opera ( Huaguxi ): A highly interactive, improvisational folk theater tradition. These shows rely on local legends, farm life, and audience interaction rather than rigid scripts. Paper Shadows: A rare form of southern Hunan shadow puppetry, featuring heavy religious rituals (like burning incense and paper money) before and after plays.

title: Hainan Lore
originalText: The Li Mother Spirit: According to ancient oral traditions, the Li people (Hainan’s earliest inhabitants) originated from a magical encounter between a Neolithic hunter and a coconut or a goddess, reflecting their deep reverence for nature. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] The Firewood-Jumping Dance: Li folklore states that when ancient ancestors were building thatched huts, the bamboo poles kept sliding off the roof. To keep the poles in place without getting their feet stabbed, people had to constantly jump. This amusing situation evolved into the iconic bamboo stick dance. Boat-Shaped Houses: To honor their seafaring ancestors who crossed the sea, the Li people build their traditional houses in the shape of boat canopies. This circular arch design deflects powerful typhoons, while elevated floors protect against moisture and jungle "miasma". Sanyuesan Festival: Known as the Double Third Festival (held on the 3rd day of the 3rd lunar month). For the Han Chinese, it is an ancestor-worship event, but for the Li and Miao, it is a massive island-wide day of love, featuring campfire singing, courtship, and bamboo dancing. 108 Brothers & Sea Gods: Hainan fishermen historically navigated the dangerous South China Sea and developed a distinct marine folklore. Joint worship of gods is prominent, with the worship of the 108 Brothers —often believed to be righteous fishermen lost at sea—being the most important aspect of their sacrificial ceremonies. Junpo Festival: Celebrated widely, particularly in regions like Hainan's northern rural areas, this indigenous festival blends Taoist rituals with village parades, where performers engage in spirit mediumship, fire-walking , and exorcisms to cleanse the community of bad luck. Temple of the Five Lords ( Wugong Temple): Located in the capital city of Haikou, this temple honors five prominent imperial officials who were banished to Hainan during the Tang and Song Dynasties. These exiled scholars brought mainland culture and folklore to the island. Gibbon Taboos: The deep emerald rainforests of Hainan—home to the highly endangered Hainan gibbon. Local traditional forest lore includes cautionary tales of hunters who kill gibbons only to suffer sudden illness or blindness, ensuring a cultural respect for local wildlife.

title: Jiangxi Lore
originalText: The Jiangshi (Chinese Hopping Vampire/Zombie): While a broad Chinese legend, the Jiangshi ("stiff corpse") or Jiangxi monster , features heavily in local village lore. These reanimated corpses are said to suck the qi (vital energy) of the living and travel by hopping stiffly across the landscape. Local tales suggest their stiff movements were inspired by ancient "corpse drivers" who used to bounce bodies across rugged terrain using bamboo rods. Nuo Dance (Ghost Drama): Originating in areas like Pingxiang, this is one of the oldest dance types of the Han Chinese. Performers wear terrifying wooden masks and engage in ritualistic "ghost dramas" to worship gods and ward off plagues and evil spirits. Jingdezhen Porcelain Lore: Known as the "Porcelain Capital of China", the city has fascinating tales dating back to the Song Dynasty (960–1279 AD). Potters historically told stories of the fierce devotion required to master their craft, with some myths attributing the flawless blue and white glazes to the magical properties of the local kaolin clays. Strange Stories from a Chinese Studio (Liaozhai Zhiyi): Many of Pu Songling’s famous tales of the supernatural—including the ghost of ghosts ( Jian ) and shape-shifting fox spirits—are heavily tied to the philosophical and mystical settings inspired by Jiangxi's Millennium Zen temples and academies.

title: Hebei Lore
originalText: The Sansei: A mischievous, one-legged mountain monster with backward-facing feet. It steals salt from miners but is easily defeated if someone yells out "Batsu" (a drought spirit). [ 1 ] Zoomorphic Deities: Traditional folk religion in the region heavily reveres the "Four Great Immortals" ( Sìdàxiān ): the Fox, Weasel, Hedgehog, and Snake Gods. They are often consulted by local shamans. 7 Xihe Dagu: Traditional drum ballads that have carried local, centuries-old stories across villages. Shadow Puppetry: Tangshan shadow plays are world-famous, bringing regional folk stories to life through intricate leather silhouettes. Lunhua: A 100-year-old intangible cultural heritage tradition where performers in Luanping County toss charcoal and iron shards into a flower, creating a spectacular cascade of sparks. Qilin Dances: In many Hebei villages, performers swap the traditional lion for the mythical Qilin (a benevolent creature) to bring prosperity and good fortune. Yuxian Paper-Cutting: A unique, 200-year-old style of paper-cutting where artisans use carving knives rather than scissors. Cangzhou's Iron Lion: A massive, over-1,000-year-old iron statue steeped in legend and local cultural pride.

title: Shandong Lore
originalText: Shandong is the legendary cradle of Chinese civilization, home to the Yellow River, Mount Tai, and the origins of Confucianism. Its rich folklore features creation myths, tales of outlaws, and sea deities that continue to shape regional culture and traditional arts. [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] 1. Mythological Origins & The Sacred Shandong is historically associated with the Dongyi people and foundational deities: Shennong (The Divine Farmer): Celebrated in carvings in Jiaxiang County, this legendary emperor is credited with teaching agriculture, inventing the plow, and tasting hundreds of herbs to discover traditional medicine. Mount Tai: The most sacred mountain in Taoism, serving as a mythological bridge between earth and the heavens. 2. The Eight Immortals & Penglai Pavilion 3. Bald-Tailed Old Li Originating in the Jiaodong peninsula, this is one of Shandong's most celebrated regional legends. It tells the story of a black dragon with a severed tail who became a rain-bringer. This folklore reflects the historical "Migration to Northeast China" from Shandong, using the dragon's journey to symbolize the migrants' longing for their homeland. [ 1 ] 4. Water Margin (Shui Hu Zhuan) One of China's Four Great Classical Novels, Water Margin is deeply rooted in Shandong's folk traditions. It romanticizes a band of 108 outlaws who gathered at Mount Liang (in Liangshan County) during the Song Dynasty to fight corrupt officials. It established archetypes of heroism and brotherhood in Chinese storytelling. 5. Han Ba (The Drought Demon) A terrifying Shandong folk monster associated with dryness and stiff corpses ( Jiangshi ). Historically, when villages suffered severe droughts, locals would search for moist graves to dig up, beat, and burn these entities as part of indigenous rainmaking customs.

title: Guizhou Lore
originalText: The Butterfly Mother: In Miao folklore, all living things and the ancestors of the Miao were birthed by the Butterfly Mother, who hatched from a maple tree. The King of Yalu: A massive oral epic of the Miao, focusing on the origins of the world, epic migrations, and mythological battles. Lusheng & Song: The Dong people are famous for their Kam Grand Songs (polyphonic choir music with no director). They are performed in Drum Towers, which are traditional wooden structures that act as community centers. Textile Epics: Because many ancient minority groups lacked a written language, they recorded their myths and family histories through intricate silverwork and embroidery. Sister's Meals Festival: A major Miao festival centered around courtship and love, celebrated in the spring with young women offering traditional colored rice to suitors. Dragon Dance with Molten Iron Fireworks: Celebrated around the Lantern Festival in Puding County, generations have passed down this tradition where performers brave molten iron sparks as a blessing for good harvests. Dixi (Ground) Opera: Known as the "living fossil" of Chinese drama, this masked opera is heavily tied to the ancient customs of the Han and Yi populations in Anshun , acting out myths and historical battles.

title: Jilin Lore
originalText: The Qilin: Known as the Chinese unicorn, this auspicious beast symbolizes good fortune, prosperity, and serenity. Legend describes it as a dragon-bodied, deer-hoofed protector that punishes the wicked and walks on clouds so it never crushes a blade of grass. Changbai Mountain Monster (Tianchi Monster): Folklore surrounding Heaven Lake at the peak of Changbai Mountain tells of a massive, lake-dwelling creature similar to the Loch Ness Monster, occasionally spotted by locals and tourists. Manchu Shamanism: Jilin is a historic heartland of Shamanic culture. Traditional shamans still act as spiritual healers and community pillars, performing rites using animal-hide drums, bird-feather headdresses, and waists adorned with dozens of bells. Northeast Folk Religion: A syncretic blend of Han Chinese settlers and Manchu traditions, focusing heavily on worship of the Fox Spirit, the Weasel (Huang Daxian), and other animal totems. Ginseng Spirits: Changbai Mountain is legendary for its wild ginseng. Local lore dictates that the "Ginseng Child" (a childlike spirit) can run away or vanish into the ground to hide from greedy harvesters. Intangible Crafts: Traditional regional arts—such as Manchu paper-cutting and northeastern "Clay Figure Zhang"—preserve historical village life, farming customs, and mythical tales. Korean Folk Heritage: In areas like Yanbian, Korean folklore heavily influences the region with vibrant agricultural dances, traditional folk games, and rhythmic pansori storytelling.

title: Yunnan Lore
originalText:  Naxi Origin Myths: The Naxi people, famous for their Dongba pictographic writing system, tell the epic legend of Sainianbao , a hero who tames nature. Their creation myth involves the separation of the sky and the earth and the origin of mankind from a brother and sister who survive a great flood. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] The Wa Wood-Drum Tradition: Central to the Wa people’s folklore is their wooden drum, which is believed to send messages to the gods. Their oral history includes tales of headhunting and primal rituals, celebrated during the Moni Carnival where mud is used as a blessing for health and long life. Dai Water Legends: The Dai people, living in the tropical river valleys of Xishuangbanna, center their folklore around water as the origin of all life. Their legends involve beautiful Peacocks, which inspire their traditional stilt houses and famous dances. Tibetan Shangri-La: The Tibetan communities in northwestern Yunnan weave myths of Shambhala with their local landscape, creating a rich oral tradition surrounding sacred snow-capped mountains (like Meili Snow Mountain), hidden valleys, and fierce protector deities. Magical Realism: Traditional stories across Yunnan are filled with supernatural characters. Prominent examples include the Lahu "head-baby" who grows up to marry an earth god’s daughter, the Kucong sisters who marry snakes, and the Tibetan mother who is reborn as a cow to aid her slave-girl daughter.

title: Guangdong Lore
originalText: Wong Fei-hung: The most famous martial artist and folk hero of the region. A master of Hung Ga kung fu, he is immortalized as a symbol of righteousness, medicine, and Southern Chinese pride. The Ten Tigers of Canton: A legendary group of ten top martial artists who defended the province against corruption and foreign invaders during the late Qing Dynasty. General Yuan (Yuan Chonghuan ): The Ming Dynasty general who defended the region against the Manchus. His famous battlefield catchphrase, "Diu nei maa, ding ying soeng !" (an incredibly fierce Cantonese exclamation), is deeply ingrained in Cantonese cultural defiance. The Southern Dragon: Unlike the imperial dragons of the north, Guangdong folklore features the dragons of the South China Sea. They are seen as patrons of the local fishermen and bringers of both rain and devastating typhoons. Black Carp ( Kuang Yu ): Deeply revered in Guangdong ponds, the black carp is a symbol of immense perseverance, strength, and overcoming adversity. Amah Rock ( Mong Fu Shek ): Located in Hong Kong (part of the historical Canton region), this is a famous stone formation. According to legend, it is the petrified body of a loyal woman holding her baby, gazing out to sea, forever waiting for her fisherman husband to return. Yingge Dance: Originating in the Chaoshan (Teochew) region, this vibrant, 300-year-old folk dance translates to "Hero's Song". Performers wear elaborate, dramatic face makeup and portray the 108 rebel heroes from the classic Chinese novel Outlaws of the Marsh . The Lion Dance: The Cantonese Lion Dance is famed globally. In folklore, the "lion" is a mythical beast believed to dispel evil spirits and bring good luck, prosperity, and rain to the harvests. Mid-Autumn Fire Dragon Dances: Performed throughout Guangdong (especially in Tai Hang), these massive, glowing dragons are paraded through the streets to rid villages of plagues and bad luck. The Goddess Mazu: Given the province's vast coastline, Mazu (the Goddess of the Sea) is the most prominent deity in Guangdong. Fishermen pray to her for safe voyages and abundant catches. Zhuji Lane Legend: Many Cantonese people trace their ancestral roots back to a specific migration point in northern Guangdong ( Nanxiong ) during the Song Dynasty. Legends of leaving this ancestral home frame much of the province's culture of diaspora, loyalty, and migration.

title: Qinghai Lore
originalText: Qinghai Lake ( Kokonor ): Considered one of the most holy lakes in Tibetan Buddhism. Devotees perform a clockwise pilgrimage around the lake, tossing ritual items like jewelry, khata (silk scarves), and grains into the waters to bless their families. [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] The Four Dragon Kings: In Chinese mythology, Qinghai Lake is historically revered as the residence of the Dragon King of the West Sea, who rules over rain and local waters. Kunlun Mountains: Qinghai's Kunlun range is the setting for the foundational Kunlun myth system. These myths are deeply intertwined with the prehistoric painted pottery of the Majiayao culture, creating a rich visual and spoken narrative of ancient spiritual civilization. Queen Mother of the West ( Xiwangmu ): Associated with the Kunlun Mountains, she is a central mythological figure in Chinese lore who holds the secrets to immortality and the elixir of life. Princess Wencheng & the Daotang River: A famous legend tells of Princess Wencheng of the Tang Dynasty travelling through Qinghai to marry King Songtsen Gampo of Tibet. Overwhelmed with homesickness near Riyue Mount, her tears supposedly flowed backward, forming the Daotang (Reversed-Flow) River. The White Camel Migration: The Salar people, a Muslim ethnic group in Qinghai, hold a migration legend. Folklore claims their ancestors followed a white camel from Central Asia to Xunhua 800 years ago, carrying one of the world's oldest handwritten Qurans. Hua'er Songs: A highly famous style of unaccompanied, improvisational folk music shared by several ethnic groups in the region. It usually features competitive, topical lyrics often centering around courtship and daily life . Guozhuang Dance: A traditional circle dance common to Tibetan communities. In these ceremonies, dancers imitate the soaring and hopping of eagles, moving rapidly to celebrate or honor religious figures. Cat Demons ( Maoguishen ): In Tu ( Monguor ) folklore, there are tales of the maoguishen (cat spirit). Historically, these spirits were sometimes believed to bring wealth to a devotee's household—but would require a shaman's exorcism ritual if they caused mysterious misfortunes.

title: Gansu Lore
originalText: Home of Fuxi: Tianshui in Gansu is historically revered as the birthplace of Fuxi , the legendary first emperor of Chinese mythology who is credited with inventing writing, fishing, and trapping. The Mother of Mankind: Legend associates Mount Niutou in Gansu with Nuwa , the goddess who molded humanity from clay and patched the heavens. Nine-Colored Deer: Originating from a famous mural in the Mogao Caves in Dunhuang, this tale follows a magnificent deer who saves a drowning man. The man betrays the deer to the king for a reward, but the deer magically exposes the betrayal, teaching a lasting moral lesson about gratitude and greed. Flying Apsaras: The enchanting flying devatas (angels) painted on the ceilings of Dunhuang are central to Gansu's folklore. They symbolize the intersection of Indian, Central Asian, and Chinese Buddhist beliefs. Hua'er Folk Songs: A celebrated musical art of Northwest China, these high-pitched, spontaneous folk songs are passed down orally. They are frequently sung in the mountains as romantic expressions or laments about rural life. Baima Tibetan Traditions: The Baima people of southern Gansu are renowned for their unique, mask-based animist dances (like the Tsangba Dance) that honor nature spirits and ancestors, accompanied by unique Tibetan lute and flute music. Thangka Painting: Tibetan communities in Gannan preserve the intricate art of Thangka. These are scroll paintings of Buddhist deities, and mastering them takes monks decades of practice. Yugur Shamanism: The Yugur people—a unique ethnic minority in Sunan—have a rich tradition of oral folklore filled with animal fables. They historically practiced shamanism, using trees, blue and white wool, and specific rituals to bridge the human and spirit worlds. Hexi Baojuan (Precious Scrolls): Originating from Dunhuang, these storytelling performances alternate between prose and verse. They act as a mix of Taoist parables, folktales, and morality plays passed down orally through the Hexi Corridor.

title: Hubei Lore
originalText: Deep in the mist-covered mountains of the Shennongjia forest reserve lives the legend of the Yeren (Chinese "Wildman"). For generations, locals have reported sightings of a large, elusive, ape-like creature covered in reddish or dark hair. The region is also named after Shennong, the mythical Divine Farmer who is said to have tasted hundreds of herbs here to discover traditional medicine. Hubei is the historical heart of the ancient State of Chu. Chu mythology is distinct and romantic, featuring a pantheon of gods, spirits, and fantastical beasts. One prominent figure is Qu Yuan, a patriotic Chu poet who threw himself into the Miluo River. His legacy birthed the Dragon Boat Festival , celebrated widely across the province with zongzi (sticky rice dumplings) and dragon boat racing . The Romance of the Three Kingdoms Many of the most famous tales from the classic 14th-century novel The Romance of the Three Kingdoms are set directly in Hubei. Important folklore sites include: Red Cliff (Chibi) The famous site of the pivotal Battle of Red Cliff where fire fleets were used to defeat Cao Cao's massive army. A historical fortress city famous for the legendary general Guan Yu. Guan Yu is venerated in Hubei as the God of War and loyalty, with many local temples still dedicated to him. The Legend of Dong Yong: Particularly popular in Xiaogan, this tale tells the story of an impoverished but filial man who sells himself into servitude to bury his father. Touched by his devotion, the Seventh Fairy Maiden (daughter of the Jade Emperor) descends from heaven to marry him, though they are ultimately torn apart by the heavens. The Story of the Yellow Crane Tower: This famous Wuhan landmark is tied to folklore of immortals and magical cranes, inspiring centuries of classical poetry.

title: Liaoning Lore
originalText: The Fox Spirit: Often viewed as clever, magical, and capable of taking human form. The Weasel (Yellow Rat): Believed to be highly spiritual and capable of either bringing good fortune or wreaking havoc if angered. The Snake (Long): Associated with protection, healing, and water. The Hedgehog & Gray Rat: Revered in domestic settings, sometimes possessing household shrines ( Xiantang or Tangzi ). "The Princess of the Moon": Predating the classic Chang'e legend, this iconic Harqin Left Wing Mongolian folklore traces the history, culture, and nomadic lifestyles of Manchurian, Mongolian, and Han groups in western Liaoning. The Hongshan Culture: Centered around Chaoyang, this 6,000-year-old prehistoric civilization is famous for unearthing the "Jade Dragon" and "Jade Owl," which gave rise to dragon and animal worship folklore still prevalent throughout China today. Shuo Bu: Epic Manchu oral narratives and heroic legends, traditionally sung with drums, narrating the origins of the Manchu people and their transition from hunting to agriculture. The geographical and environmental landscapes of Liaoning—spanning the Bohai Sea, coastal wetlands, and the Changbai Mountains (locally known as Dongshanli )—have birthed regional legends. Stories frequently focus on water deities, animal protectors of the forest, and mythological manifestations like the Kui Niu (a powerful, one-legged mythical creature that symbolizes strength and protection). Folklore in Liaoning is actively preserved through regional performance arts and rituals, t hese include: Yangge Dance: A vibrant, rhythmic, and acrobatic stilt and group dance used to invoke gods and celebrate bountiful harvests (such as the Quanbao Cunqiao Yangge in Benxi). Shadow Puppetry: Traditional folk dramas and folktales told using intricate shadow puppets, heavily popular in cities like Shenyang and Liaoyang. Suona and Drum Music: Traditional wind and percussion music used in both celebratory and sacred folkloric ceremonies.

title: Zhejiang Lore
originalText: The Butterfly Lovers (Liang Zhu): Originating in Ningbo and Hangzhou, this is one of China's Four Great Folktales. It follows Zhu Yingtai, who disguises herself as a male scholar to get an education. She falls in love with her classmate Liang Shanbo. Forbidden to marry, Liang dies of a broken heart. When Zhu's funeral procession passes his grave, it opens, and the two lovers’ souls emerge as butterflies, flying away together. The Legend of the White Snake (Baishe Zhuan): Set primarily at Hangzhou's West Lake and the Leifeng Pagoda, this tale features a white snake spirit who transforms into a beautiful woman named Bai Suzhen. She falls in love with a mortal man, Xu Xian. Their romance is constantly disrupted by a conservative Buddhist monk, Fahai, who eventually imprisons Bai under the pagoda. Legends of Great Yu & Fangfeng: Deep in the mountainous terrain of northern Zhejiang lies the legacy of Yu the Great, who tamed ancient floods. Local folklore heavily features the myth of Fangfeng, an ancestral giant and tutelary spirit of the region. Historically, Yu executed Fangfeng for arriving late to a flood-control assembly, but local temples in Zhejiang revere Fangfeng as an exonerated local hero. Sericulture and the Legend of Leizu: The Jiangnan region (including Zhejiang) is the heartland of Chinese silk production. Folklore credits Empress Leizu, the wife of the Yellow Emperor, with discovering silk when a silkworm cocoon dropped into her tea. This legend birthed a rich tapestry of local sericulture taboos and rituals practiced in Zhejiang's silk towns. Dragon Worship & Dances: Rooted in the Xin'an River Basin, "Loong" (dragon) culture isa massive part of Zhejiang folk tradition. Colorful festivals frequently feature unique local performances like the grass loongs , bench loongs , and fish lantern loongs . Local Diet & Customs: Seasonal folk rituals heavily dictate life. During Lixia (the start of summer), locals practice folk customs centering around specific foods, such as eating wumifan (black glutinous rice) to protect against summer heat and illnesses. Nature Spirits: Rooted in early localized folklore, everyday physical landmarks in Zhejiang (such as rivers, mountains, and trees) are believed to harbor their own ancient spirits, deities, or "Yaoguai" (monsters), which demand reverence and respect.

title: Heilongjiang Lore
originalText: The name "Heilongjiang" translates to "Black Dragon River". Local legend holds that a malevolent white dragon wreaked havoc and caused suffering. A brave young man transformed into a black dragon to fight the white dragon, eventually defeating it. The black dragon died in the conflict, and its body became the mighty river that brings flourishing natural resources and luck to the region. One of the most famous figures in Northeast China's folklore is "Bald-Tailed Old Li". According to the tale, he was born as a black dragon in Shandong to the Li family, but had his tail severed by his frightened father. He flew north to Heilongjiang, where he helped local migrants defeat a wicked white dragon and became the region's benevolent river god. This legend reflects the historical "Migration to Northeast China" and embodies the nostalgia and regional identity of Shandong migrants. The Hezhe people, an indigenous group residing where the Heilong and Songhua rivers meet, have a UNESCO-listed oral tradition called Yimakan . This art form involves a mix of speaking and singing without musical accompaniment. Yimakan stories are passed down through generations to preserve the history, spirituality, and culture of the clan. Mergen Heroes: The tales focus on heroes called Mergen , symbols of wisdom and unmatched skill in fishing and hunting. As the historical heartland of the Manchu, Heilongjiang is home to a vast collection of myths detailing creation, clan migrations, and ancestral spirits. Manchu epic storytelling features composite narrative structures with themes ranging from cosmic battles of three goddesses to the adventures of tribal heroes.

title: Shanxi Lore
originalText: The Foolish Old Man (Yugong): Originating from the Taihang Mountains (which form the eastern border of Shanxi), this famous legend tells of an old man who stubbornly decided to move two massive mountains obstructing his path, inspiring generations with his perseverance. The Four Dragons of Jincheng: Local folklore centers heavily around deities protecting the rugged land, with deep ties to Taoist and Buddhist cosmologies that were historically preserved in remote temples. Yellow River Spirits: Tales of the swirling Yellow River—the lifeblood of Shanxi—abound, featuring localized water spirits, mythical monsters, and deities meant to protect communities from floods. Shehuo (Social Fires): A centuries-old, traditional folk entertainment popular during the Chinese New Year. It features dragon dances, lion dances, acrobatics, and stilt walking, historically held to thank gods for a past harvest and pray for the next. Folk Arts: Shanxi is famous for its intricate, lace-like paper-cutting , traditional wood-embroidered shoes, and Kang paintings (a distinct folk art decorating village brick beds). Folksongs: Shanxi is divided into three primary folk music genres: Shan'ge (mountain songs reflecting rural life), Xiaodiao (melodic and familiar little tunes), and Chang'ge (long narrative songs). Oral Literature: The province has a deeply rooted oral storytelling tradition, with recorded local folklore tales detailing heroes, moral fables, and supernatural foxes.

title: Anhui Lore
originalText: The Ao Fish ( Aoyu ): Originating from Huangshan and Tangmo villages, this legendary creature possesses a dragon’s head and a fish’s body. Folklore says a massive Aoyu carries Mount Tai on its back, and spotting a floating Aoyu lantern in the night sky brings peace and good fortune. Zhong Kui: Hailing from Lingbi county, Zhong Kui is a fierce deity from Chinese mythology famous for vanquishing ghosts and evil spirits. In Anhui folklore, his legend is intrinsically tied to local craftsmanship, as local artisans immortalize his image by carving him out of rare Lingbi black stones. Mount Huang's Immortals: The Yellow Emperor (Huangdi) is said to have ascended the peaks of Mount Huang to gather medicinal herbs and successfully forge pills of immortality. Wuwei Fish Lanterns: Celebrated for over 600 years, this provincial-level Intangible Cultural Heritage features glowing, colorful fish-shaped lanterns parading through the streets, especially during the Spring Festival and Lantern Festival. Taige Parades: A spectacular folk tradition historically performed in Shouxian County. It involves adults and children in elaborate makeup and costumes balancing on moving, elevated platforms to act out dramatic scenes from Chinese lore. Huaguxi (Flower-drum Opera): Originating primarily from the northern city of Bozhou , this traditional folk opera features playful local dialects, songs, and dances that tell stories of rural life, harvest, and love. Huizhou Architecture: Ancient Anhui villages—such as Hongcun and Xidi —are deeply rooted in Fengshui and Taoist harmony with nature, seamlessly blending mountain landscapes with curved, flying-eaves rooflines. Four Treasures of the Study: Anhui's folklore and arts are connected through the invention of traditional calligraphy tools. The story goes that craftsmen in ancient Xuancheng invented Xuan Paper to perfectly preserve ink, allowing artists to record myths and local folklore across generations.

title: Shaanxi Lore
originalText: Xintianyou : A genre of mountain folk songs requiring a clear, sincere voice. These are passed down orally and tell the real-life struggles of farming, poverty, and love. Sanxian Shu: A Northern Shaanxi storytelling art where performers sing and recount legends while playing a three-stringed lute ( sanxian ). Shadow Puppetry: Intricate, hand-carved leather figures acting out legendary Chinese tales—like The Monkey King —accompanied by local music. Shehuo : An ancient, elaborate folk performance originating from sacrificial ceremonies. Performers wear terrifying, vibrant, traditional masks (such as "Horse Ladle" facial makeup) intended to ward off evil spirits and bring good harvests. Paper-Cutting (Jianzhi): Widely practiced in rural communities like Yanchuan County, women pass these detailed, symmetrical designs through generations to decorate windows and celebrate the seasons. Embroidered Patchwork: Vibrant textiles, including tiger-head shoes and pillows, made to protect children and invite blessings. The "Ten Weirdos of Guanzhong" Central Shaanxi (the Guanzhong Plain) is famous for its humorous folklore known as the "Ten Weirdos." This oral tradition playfully highlights the unique local climate, geography, and diet: Noodles like belts: Belt-wide biangbiang noodles. Houses like half houses: Slanted, single-slope roof structures. Girls not walking out in public: Headscarves used to shield women from loess dust. Crying, not singing, for marriage: Traditional wedding laments.

title: Serbia Lore
originalText: Zmaj: A benevolent, wise winged dragon or serpent that protects tribes, brings rain, and fights evil. Ala: A malevolent, storm-bringing demon or multi-headed dragon enemy that ruins crops. Vila: Wild, beautiful female forest fairies associated with natural springs and prophetic powers. Baš Čelik: A famous steel-coated villain/ogre king from fairy tales representing trapped immortal strength. Kosovo Myth: A central national narrative centered on the 1389 Battle of Kosovo, where Prince Lazar chose a heavenly kingdom over earthly victory. Epic Songs: Oral poems sung to the accompaniment of the gusle , recounting heroic feats by figures like Marko Kraljević and Miloš Obilić. Kolo: A traditional, fast-paced circular group dance protected as intangible cultural heritage. Opanak: Traditional, laced-free leather shoes featuring a distinct upward-curved toe.

title: Cyprus Lore
originalText: Birth of Aphrodite: The island's most famous myth. The goddess of love and beauty is said to have risen from the sea foam near Petra tou Romiou (Aphrodite's Rock) off the coast of Paphos. According to tradition, swimming around the rock on a full moon grants eternal youth and beauty. Digenis Akritas: The quintessential Cypriot hero. This fearless, half-Arab and half-Byzantine warrior is famed for his supernatural strength. Legend says he created the Pentadaktylos (Five Finger) mountain range in North Cyprus by leaving his handprint as he leapt across the sea to defend the island. King Pygmalion & Galatea: The ancient king of Cyprus who, disillusioned by mortal women, sculpted a statue so perfect he fell in love with it. He prayed to Aphrodite to bring her to life, and his wish was granted. The Kallikantzaroi: Mischievous, goblin-like creatures believed to live underground for most of the year. They emerge during the 12 days of Christmas to wreak havoc on households, only to retreat underground on the Epiphany. Ayia Napa Sea Serpent: A local monster that dwells in the waters of Cape Greco . Described as half-crocodile and half-serpent, it is said to have been spotted since Roman times and is known to locals as a gentle protector of the sea. Kataklysmos: The Festival of the Flood, celebrating the story of Noah's Ark as well as the birth of Aphrodite. Celebrated 50 days after Orthodox Easter in coastal cities like Larnaca , it features water-fights, folk dancing, and sea-sports. Dragons of the Heartland: Stemming from a blend of myth and St. George, village fountains throughout Cyprus feature tales of dragons and mythical beasts. Cypriot folklore is brought to life through traditional instruments like the violin and laouto (lute). Folk dances such as the Karsilama (a face-to-face dance between couples) and Sirto (a circular wrist-hold dance) are staples of village weddings and communal gatherings.

title: Denmark Lore
originalText: Nisse: A mischievous but loyal farm spirit. No taller than a child and wearing a traditional red cap, he protects the household if treated with respect but wreaks havoc if offended. [ 1 ] Trolls: Enormous, ancient beings made of stone and earth who live deep in the forests or beneath hills. They are famously afraid of daylight and church bells, which turn them into stone. Elverfolk (Elves): Seductive, ethereal dancers who inhabit mounds and misty bogs at night. Humans are warned not to join their magical dances, which can cause them to lose their minds or be trapped in the earth forever. Valravn: A monstrous shape-shifting raven born on blood-stained battlefields. It possesses molten gold eyes and can mimic human voices or transform into a human. It feeds on greed and human sorrow, preying on lost travelers. Kirke-Grim (Church Grim): A guardian spirit (often a black dog or pig) attached to local churches. It protects the building and graveyard from dark spirits and watches over the parish. King Skjold: The mythical founder of the Danish royal lineage (the Scylding dynasty). According to legend, he arrived as an abandoned baby on a boat filled with treasures and grew up to become a mighty king. Gefjon: A powerful goddess who tricked the Swedish king into giving her land. She plowed the Swedish earth with her four ox-sons to carve out the large island of Zealand, leaving behind Lake Mälaren. Holger Danske (Ogier the Dane): Denmark's most celebrated legendary hero. According to the myths, he never truly died but rests deep in the casemates of Kronborg Castle. He sleeps, but will awaken and come to Denmark's defense in its darkest hour of need. Denmark has a rich history of oral folklore, meticulously collected in the 19th century by scholars like Svend Grundtvig and E.T. Kristensen, which inspired world-famous fairy tales written by Hans Christian Andersen, such as "The Little Mermaid" and "The Steadfast Tin Soldier" .

title: South Africa Lore
originalText: Grootslang: A colossal elephant-headed, serpent-bodied monster said to dwell in a deep cave (the "Wonder Hole") in the Richtersveld, fiercely guarding a hoard of diamonds. Inkanyamba: A massive, carnivorous river serpent believed by the Zulu people to live in the deep pools near waterfalls, such as Howick Falls, capable of stirring up fierce storms. Antjie Somers: A popular Cape folklore bogeyman—often described as a man who dresses in women's clothing—used to frighten disobedient children into behaving. Tokoloshe: A mischievous and wicked dwarf-like spirit in Zulu mythology that can become invisible and cause trouble or illness unless bed legs are raised off the ground. The Hare: The ultimate clever hero of southern African animal tales, frequently outwitting larger, more powerful adversaries like the lion or elephant. The Jackal: Portrayed as cunning, slick, and self-serving, often matching wits or competing directly with the hare and the lion. The Tortoise: Uses slow and steady cleverness to navigate out of tight spots created by his own or others' mischief. The Praying Mantis (Cagn): Regarded by the San people as a vital divine creator figure, culture hero, and messenger from the spiritual realm. Stellar Lore: Indigenous groups across the region held distinct beliefs about the heavens; for instance, the Karanga viewed stars as the eyes of the dead, while other groups thought them to be holes in a solid rock sky.

title: Welsh Lore
originalText: Four Branches of the Mabinogi : Medieval prose tales detailing heroes like Pryderi, Rhiannon, and Bran the Blessed. Math fab Mathonwy : The story of the powerful wizard Gwydion and his nephew Lleu Llaw Gyffes. Culhwch and Olwen : One of the oldest Arthurian tales featuring a massive hunt for the wild boar Twrch Trwyth . The Welsh Triads : Short groups of three items used by bards to preserve tribal history, heroes, and ancient lore. Tylwyth Teg : The fair folk or underground and underwater fairies known to swap human babes for changelings. Afanc : A fierce lake monster resembling a giant beaver or crocodile. Cŵn Annwn : Spectral hounds of the Otherworld whose booming barks signal upcoming death. Ceffyl Dŵr : A shape-shifting , flying water-horse spirit. Coblynau : Small, gnome-like miners who guide humans to rich ore veins or cause rockfalls. Y Ddraig Goch : The red dragon of Wales said to reside at Dinas Emrys, battling the white dragon. Cantre'r Gwaelod : The legendary sunken "Welsh Atlantis" lost to the sea due to drunken negligence. Beddgelert : The touching and tragic grave site of a faithful hound belonging to Prince Llywelyn.

title: Mauritania Lore
originalText: The Ighyuwn : Traditional entertainer caste functioning as singers, poets, clowns, and social historians. Occult Reputation: Historically feared and respected as keepers of secret knowledge and hidden powers. Fables and Proverbs: Short moral fables passed down through generations in the Hassaniya dialect. Whispering Dunes: Desert legends warn travelers of phantom voices and shifting sands that lead the proud or impatient astray. The Jinn : Invisible desert spirits believed to play tricks on lone voyagers crossing the vast Sahara. Azawan : A unique traditional musical system said to draw aesthetic inspiration from the calls of desert birds. Folk Instruments: Performance centered around the tidinit (a traditional Moorish guitar) and the ardin (a harp-like instrument). The Tea Ritual: The symbolic three-pour tea ceremony ( atay ) embodying hospitality, patience, and community connection.

title: Guinea Lore
originalText: 1. The Epic Hero: Sunjata (Sundiata) Perhaps the most famous figure in Guinean and broader West African lore is Sunjata Keita , the legendary founder of the 13th-century Mali Empire. [ 1 , 2 ] Born unable to walk, Sunjata endured years of scorn and mocking from his father's other wives. After a particularly cruel insult to his mother, a young Sunjata grabbed an iron rod and pulled himself to his feet, famously breaking the rod as he stood up. He th e n went on to defeat the sorcerer-king Soumaoro Kanté at the Battle of Kirina, uniting the Mandinka people and shaping the cultural and historical backbone of the region's folklore. Death and His Son-In-Law: A prominent Malinké creation myth centers on Sa (Death), who lived with his family before humans existed. The story explains the origins of human mortality and how the earth was eventually opened up to new life, with the rooster serving as the animal that welcomes the morning. The Buffalo of Dô: A foundational myth among the Malinké involves two hunter brothers who embark on a quest to kill the fearsome Buffalo of Dô. The tale introduces the mystical elements, sacrifices, and magical prophecies required to establish great lineages and empires. The Ninimini (River Dragon): Widespread in West African and Guinean river folklore, the Ninimini is a massive, serpentine water spirit or swamp dragon. In some tellings, it is considered a dangerous, powerful guardian of the river depths. Forest and Water Spirits: For many Guinean communities, deep forests and untamed natural landmarks are believed to be inhabited by powerful nature spirits that demand respect. Mocking these spirits almost always leads to a cautionary lesson . 4. Sacred Rituals and Masks In Guinea, folklore is not just spoken; it is performed through sacred dances, elaborate costuming, and collective rituals. Soli Wulen (The Red Panther): In Malinké folklore, the Soli Wulen is a sacred, otherworldly figure covered in dense red fibers, mirrors, and protective charms. It appears during community initiation ceremonies to guard young initiates from harmful spirits. Konden: An imposing and spectacular figure in Malinké culture, Konden wears elaborate costumes and exaggerated facial features. Used during communal rituals, it represents spirits and mythological warriors, creating powerful energy that brings the ancient stories to life.

title: Greek Lore
originalText: The Primordials & Titans: Creation began with Chaos, giving rise to Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Sky). Their Titan children, led by Cronus, ruled the cosmos until overthrown by the Olympian gods in the Titanomachy. The Olympians: The twelve Olympian gods, led by Zeus, shaped the moral and physical world, influencing everything from war and harvest to the arts. Heroes & Monsters: Enduring tales feature heroes like Odysseus and Theseus battling mythological threats such as the Minotaur, Medusa, and the deadly whirlpool Charybdis. Demotic Music: Modern Greek folk music evolved from Byzantine and ancient roots. Regional instruments define the sound, such as the Cretan lyra , mainland clarinets, and bagpipes in Macedonia. Mourning Songs ( Mirolóyia ): A cappella laments traditionally sung by older women in the Epirus and Mani regions to honor the dead. Folk Customs: Practices are often tied to the land and religion, such as placing copper coins over the eyes of the deceased or passing babies around the hearth for protection.

title: Jordan Lore
originalText: Jinn and Trial Tales: Folktales often involve trials between humans and jinn , or dialogues with the dead. They explain natural phenomena or cosmologic creations. [ 1 ] The Bedouin Tradition: Bedouin folklore is deeply rooted in the desert, focusing on bravery, hospitality, and the protection of travelers. The Dabke: This famous Levantine line dance is a staple of Jordanian celebrations, featuring loud ground-pounding leg movements accompanied by traditional instruments like the Oud and Rebab . The Lost City of Petra: The Nabataean city was lost to the West for centuries. Local folklore claims the Siq (the narrow gorge) and the Khazneh (The Treasury) were carved by the wand of Moses to bring forth water for the Israelites. The Cave of the Seven Sleepers: Located near Amman, this site tells the story of righteous youths who sought refuge in a cave and slept for centuries to escape religious persecution. The Dead Sea: Legends suggest the mineral-rich mud and warm waters of the lowest point on Earth were the beauty secrets of Cleopatra and a favored retreat of King Herod.

title: Bosnia and Herzegovina Lore
originalText: Vila: Radiant mountain fairies who live in dense forests, sing, and help—or test—heroes. [ 1 , 2 ] Zmaj & Aždaha: The Zmaj is a noble, weather-controlling dragon, while the Aždaha is a destructive, multi-headed monster representing chaos. Mora & Drekavac : The Mora is a spirit that sits on sleeping chests to cause nightmares, while the Drekavac is the shrieking, tragic ghost of an unbaptized child. Tur: According to Central Bosnian folklore, the Tur is a colossal mythical bull holding the world on its horns. Earthquakes happen whenever he moves. Sevdalinka : A legendary genre of folk music deeply influenced by the Ottoman era. It is heavily emotive, often telling tragic, aching stories of separated lovers. Kolo: The traditional, fast-paced line dance performed at weddings and festivals. In some regions, the Silent Kolo is performed without any instruments; dancers use the rhythmic stomping of their feet and the clinking of silver coins on their traditional aprons to keep the beat. Traditional clothing—like the famous Zmijanje embroidery—is woven with heavy silk and features intricate geometric designs in red, black, and gold. Women’s outfits are heavily adorned with silver coins, beads, and woven aprons.

title: Mongolia Lore
originalText: Tengri: The supreme god of the eternal blue sky, creator of all things and father of early rulers. Etugen Eke: The Mother Earth goddess, representing fertility, land, and the life of nature. Erlik Khan: The ruler of the underworld and king of death, associated with sickness and subterranean forces. Epic Literature and Legends The Secret History of the Mongols: The 13th-century foundational chronicle beginning with the ancestry of a blue-gray wolf and a fallow deer. Epic of King Gesar (Geser): A massive Central Asian and Mongol religious epic about a prophetic warrior-king of Tengriism and Buddhism. Jangar : A heroic epic detailing the exploits of brave warriors and their utopian land of Bumba. Manggus : Multi-headed malevolent monsters often defeated by culture heroes or clever tricksters. Erkhii Mergen: The tale of an arrogant archer who missed a shot at the sun and vowed to cut off his thumb if he failed, becoming the marmot. The Camel Versus the Mouse: An animal fabled explanation of why the camel lacks front teeth and why the camel rolls in ashes regarding the lunar calendar.

title: Brunei Lore
originalText: Jong Batu: A rock outcrop in the Brunei River shaped like a sinking ship. It is the core of the Nakhoda Manis (Captain Sweet) legend, which tells the tale of an unfilial son whose ship was cursed and turned to stone by his mother. [ 1 , 2 ] Pulau Pilong-Pilongan & Lumut Lunting: Two islands/sandbanks in the Brunei Bay associated with ancient folklore and the early beginnings of the Sultanate. The Golden Mountain and the Weeping Rice: A classic myth about a magical, treasure-filled mountain that sought to bless a generous society, but sailed away forever upon hearing the cries of a neglected, weeping community. Awang Alak Betatar: The legendary founder of Brunei. According to tradition, he was originally a local prince who became the first Sultan of Brunei (Sultan Muhammad Shah) after winning a historic boat race and converting to Islam. Tujuh Telaga Mandian Puteri: A Tutong legend about two heavenly princesses who flew down from Mount Mulu to bathe in seven hidden sand-wells during every full moon. Nakhoda Ragam: The tale of a mighty Sultan and warrior whose unyielding spirit lives on in local legends tied to the mysterious three-tomb site in Brunei Darussalam. Nature Spirits and Guardian Trees: Ancient, large spiral trees often feature in urban legends as being guarded by, or containing, vengeful or protective spirits of the land. Hantu Penanggalan & Hantu Raya: Like much of Bornean ghost lore, Brunei folklore features supernatural spirits. The Penanggalan is a vampiric woman whose head detaches at night, and the Hantu Raya is a giant guardian spirit that can be bound by a master.

title: Croatian Lore
originalText: Vila: Magical, blonde-haired forest fairies who possess healing powers but can be wrathful if provoked. Krsnik: A benevolent shaman or vampire hunter who protects humans from dark magic. Mora: An evil spirit or nightmare that suffocates victims in their sleep. Štriga & Vukodlak : The Croatian equivalents of witches and werewolves, often associated with dark magic, bad luck, or the undead. Domaci & Malik: Tiny, mischievous house or forest spirits that can bring good luck or play pranks. The Black Queen: A legendary ruler who brought rain to a drought-stricken land, creating the stunning terraced waters of the Plitvice Lakes National Park.
