[ 1 , 2 , 3 ]  Moko -Jumbies : Spirits dancing atop 6-to-8-foot stilts in colorful gowns and tall headpieces, rooted in African tradition symbolizing protection and gods of vengeance.  Clown Troupes: Performers in baggy, bell-adorned clothing and pink wire-mesh masks who dance to string band music, paced by the cracking of a leather hunter’s whip.  Obeah : A traditional system of spiritual beliefs, herbal medicine, and regional black magic deeply tied to the islands' historical folklore and superstitions.

title: Kiribati Lore
originalText: Na Areau (The Spider God): The ultimate creator. In ancient times, he wove the cosmos from a vast, endless space, bringing the first sky and earth into being. The Tree of Life: Te Kaintikuaba is the sacred tree from which the first spirits originated in Samoa before migrating north to populate the coral atolls. Separating the Earth and Sky: To make room for the world to grow, Na Areau had Riiki (the Eel) stretch himself between the darkness of the earth and the heavens to push the sky upwards. Nei Tituaabine: A beautiful red-haired woman and tree goddess. When she passed away, three sacred trees grew from her resting place: a coconut from her head, a pandanus from her heels, and an almond from her navel. Auriaria: A red-haired giant demigod who fell in love with Nei Tituaabine, representing the divine connection between the people, the land, and the sea. The Singing Fish: Folktales often highlight the harmony between humans and the ocean. Legends like the Singing Fish teach I-Kiribati children about environmental respect, gratitude, and the consequences of human greed. Trickster Magic: Stories often revolve around clever underdogs—such as the "brave little tailor" archetype—who use trickery and resourcefulness to outsmart man-eating witches ( hag ), monsters, or greedy giants. Kinship and Survival: Many tales focus on siblings and families relying on cooperation and ingenuity to endure harsh environments and threatening entities. The Maneaba: Much of this folklore was passed down orally under the roof of the maneaba (traditional meeting house) by village elders ( Unim'ane ). Dance ( Te Kaimatoa & Te Buki ): Traditional dances mimic the movements of the frigate bird and ocean waves. The bird itself serves as a central symbol in many coastal tales, acting as a divine navigator and a sign of peace.

title: Dominican Republic Lore
originalText: La Ciguapa : Perhaps the most famous Dominican mythical creature, the Ciguapa is a nocturnal woman with long, dark hair and backward-facing feet, making her footprints impossible to track. She is said to live in the deep mountain forests, often luring men into the woods before making them disappear. El Galipote : A shape-shifting man who can transform into animals (such as a black dog, or Lugarú ) or inanimate objects like trees and rocks. Galipotes are known for their immense strength, cruelty, and immunity to firearms. El Bacá : A devilish, shape-shifting animal familiar (often a black dog or bull with glowing red eyes) created through black magic. It grants wealth, land, or protection to its owner, but requires the soul of a loved one or material sacrifices in return. Las Brujas (Witches): European-derived tales of women who make pacts with the devil, allowing them to fly, cast curses, and transform into large birds. Las 21 Divisiones : This is the primary folk religion of the Dominican Republic. Rooted deeply in West African Vodou traditions, it classifies spirits into distinct "divisions" (like Rada, Petro, and Gede). It also incorporates Taíno ancestral spirits and is practiced alongside Catholicism. Los Indios de las Aguas: Harmless, generous spirits that live in rivers, lakes, and underwater caves. They are believed to be the ancient Taíno inhabitants and are known for their extensive knowledge of herbal medicine. Taíno Resistance: The island's original folklore reveres historical figures like Enriquillo , a Taíno cacique (chief) who fought Spanish colonial oppression, and Anacaona , a revered Taíno queen and poet. Carnival: Dominican Carnival (celebrated heavily in February and March) brings folklore to life. It features iconic characters like the Diablo Cojuelo (limping devil) who playfully whips spectators, and the Taimáscaros of Puerto Plata, which blend Taíno and African masks to celebrate the island's dual heritage.

title: Liechtenstein Lore
originalText: The Three Sisters (Drei Schwestern): This tale explains the origin of the striking rock formation high above the Rhine Valley. Three young sisters skipped church on Lady’s Day (August 15) to go berry picking. When they refused to share their berries with a beautiful woman, she turned them into the three giant rocks that stand as the Drei Schwestern mountain chain today. The Lochgass Horse: Legend tells of a horse thief in Vaduz who stole a beautiful white horse on Christmas Eve. The animal, which was the Devil in disguise, rode the man wildly across the valley before throwing him and breaking his neck. The Golden Boos: This popular tale features a stout woman carrying a chest on her back. When she stops at an inn, a small man climbs out of the chest and robs the place blind. The Guschg Herdsmen's Doll: Herdsmen spending the summer in mountain cabins crafted a life-size rag doll to entertain themselves. In the autumn, the doll came to life and demanded one herdsman stay with her. She subsequently skinned him and hung his skin on the cottage roof to dry, sitting next to it and laughing. The Wildmannli: Known as the "Wild Men," these are fur-covered, bear-like creatures from the mountains who wore no clothes. They were generally helpful, often caring for cattle, calling local midwives when needed, and turning coal into shiny coins for good people. Hans Jöri: During the intense witch hunts of the 17th century, the region generated tales of witchcraft. A famous legend details a fiddler who unknowingly played at a witches' party. When he refused to toast to the Devil and instead toasted to himself, the witches vanished, and he awoke at a scaffold holding a bleeding ox's hoof.

title: Latvian Lore
originalText: Dievs : The supreme god of the sky and the ultimate creator. Laima: The revered goddess of fate, luck, and destiny who determines the length of human life. Māra: The earth mother and protector of women, nature, and the home. Pērkons : The powerful god of thunder, war, and fertility. Saule & Mēness : The personified Sun (female) and Moon (male) deities, who feature heavily in cosmic wedding stories. " Mātes " (Mothers): Various female nature spirits governing the elements, such as Jūras māte (Mother of the Sea), Vēja māte (Mother of the Wind), and Lauku māte (Mother of the Fields). Lāčplēsis (The Bear Slayer): The iconic national epic created by Andrejs Pumpurs. Born to a human mother and a bear father, Lāčplēsis possesses superhuman strength and fights dark crusaders to defend Latvia. Lieldienas (Spring Equinox): Celebrates the rebirth of nature. Traditions include the dyeing and rolling of eggs to ensure fertility. Jāņi (Summer Solstice): The most significant cultural holiday. People weave wreaths of oak leaves and wildflowers, light massive bonfires, and search for the mythical "fern flower" on the shortest night of the year.

title: Iceland Lore
originalText: Unlike the short, pointy-eared elves in pop culture, the huldufólk are human-sized, beautiful beings who live in rocks, cliffs, and hills. Habitat: They are invisible to the human eye unless they choose to reveal themselves, often on New Year's Eve or the summer solstice. Road Construction: Many Icelandic roads are diverted around massive boulders or hills to avoid disturbing the hidden people. You can even find tiny wooden houses, called álfhóll , built for elves to inhabit. In Icelandic legends, trolls are colossal, often slow-witted giants who reside in the harsh mountains. The Rules of Daylight: Trolls are petrified (turned into stone) if they are exposed to the sun's rays. Specific Locations: This legend is used to explain many of Iceland's strange rock formations. For example, the striking Reynisdrangar sea stacks off the coast of Vík are said to be the silhouettes of two trolls who were caught by the morning sun while attempting to haul a ship to shore. The Troll Gateway: The dark Dimmuborgir lava field in northern Iceland is frequently described as the gateway to Hell and the home of the most famous troll parents, Grýla and Leppalúði. Grýla and the Cat: Grýla is a terrifying, child-devouring ogress who prowls the winter countryside for misbehaving children. She is accompanied by the Jólakötturinn (Yule Cat), a giant feline that eats anyone who doesn't receive new clothes for Christmas. The 13 Yule Lads: Grýla’s 13 sons visit human settlements one by one in the 13 nights leading up to Christmas. While they were originally malevolent pranksters, today they leave small gifts in children's shoes (or rotting potatoes for those who misbehave). The Land Wights ( Landvættir ): These are the four mythical guardians that protect the four quarters of Iceland: a dragon in the east, a griffin in the north, a bull in the west, and a mountain giant in the south. They were even said to have frightened away a sorcerer attempting to invade Iceland in the form of a whale. Lake Monsters: The Lagarfljót Worm in east Iceland is an aquatic monster similar to the Loch Ness Monster, while maritime tales abound of terrifying sea creatures known as skrímsli .

title: Lebanese Lore
originalText: Astarte & Adonis: A famous Phoenician love myth. Adonis, a handsome mortal hunter, was fatally wounded by a boar. The goddess of love, Astarte (Aphrodite), mourned his death, and the blood-red river, Nahr Ibrahim (the Adonis River), is said to flow from his wounds every spring. Jinn & Ghouls: Folk beliefs frequently feature Jinn (shapeshifting spirits) residing in abandoned places, like the famously eerie village of Wata Sfarta . Ghouls (flesh-eating creatures) haunt graveyards and isolated areas. Abu Keis (Father of the Bag): A spooky figure who wandered the streets with a large sack, snatching up children who stayed outside too late. Em R3di (Mother of Thunder): A terrifying character used to scare kids into coming indoors during severe thunderstorms. Monsieur Sale: A bogeyman figure used to warn children about the dangers of being unhygienic or playing in the dirt. The Hakawati : Traditional storytellers who used to entertain crowds in local cafes with epics like 1001 Nights , typically keeping listeners hooked with dramatic cliffhangers. Dabke: The legendary traditional line dance performed at weddings and community gatherings. It is accompanied by folk instruments like the oud (lute) and mijwiz (wind instrument). Folklore Attire: While almost everyone wears modern clothing today, traditional costumes include the Sherwal (baggy pants for men) and the historical Tantour (a tall, cone-shaped headdress historically worn by women). Pearls on a Branch: A prominent collection of 100 translated Arabic folktales collected from elderly female storytellers across Lebanon. Proverbs: Traditional Lebanese sayings are central to the culture. They are usually satirical or parodic and provide insight into the historic social and patriarchal structures of the country.

title: Ireland Lore
originalText: The Mythological Cycle: Details the arrival of ancient races and the Tuatha Dé Danann—a pantheon of skilled gods and goddesses who governed the land before retreating into the subterranean otherworld to become the Faerie Folk. The Ulster Cycle: The Irish equivalent to Greek epics, focusing on the heroic feats of Cú Chulainn (the Hound of Ulster) and Queen Medb's legendary Cattle Raid of Cooley ( Táin Bó Cúailnge ). The Fenian (Ossianic) Cycle: Chronicles the adventures of Finn McCool ( Fionn mac Cumhaill ) and his band of warriors, the Fianna. The Historical Cycle: Blends myth and pseudo-history to chronicle the ancient High Kings of Ireland, focusing heavily on political lineage and the seat of power at the Hill of Tara. The Children of Lir: A jealous stepmother turns four royal children into swans, condemning them to wander the lakes of Ireland for 900 years. Diarmuid and Grainne: A tragic romance in which a legendary warrior and a princess break a royal engagement to run away, leading to a relentless, continent-wide pursuit. The Salmon of Knowledge: Finn McCool tastes an enchanted fish that grants him universal wisdom, kickstarting his legendary career. The Aos Sí (or Sidhe): The fairy folk believed to be the descendants of the Tuatha Dé Danann, inhabiting ancient mounds and hills. The Banshee ( Bean Sídhe ): A female spirit whose mournful wail or keening is an omen that death is approaching a specific family. The Púka : A shape-shifting trickster spirit that can bring either great good fortune or immense mischief to those who cross its path. The Dullahan: A terrifying, headless horseman who rides through the night carrying his own head, serving as an omen of death. The Leprechaun: Rooted in old myths about a fairy cobbler, he is known for hoarding pots of gold at the end of the rainbow. Changeling: A faerie child secretly left in a human cradle to replace a human baby that has been stolen by the faeries.

title: Venezuelan Lore
originalText: El Silbón (The Whistler): A tall, spectral figure from the plains ( Llanos ) who carries a sack of bones and whistles a chilling musical note that foreshadows death. La Sayona: A vengeful female phanto m in a long white dress who appears to unfaithful men to terrify or punish them. Florentino el que Cantó con el Diablo: A legendary llanero singer who famously defeated the Devil in an improvised folk singing duel ( contrapunteo ). María Lionza: A major nature goddess and queen of a prominent spiritual cult, often depicted riding a tapir and revered at Sorte Mountain. Amalivaca: The creator god of the Warao and Tamanaco peoples who shaped the Orinoco river landscape. Makunaima: A trickster and culture hero central to the mythology of the Pemón indigenous people. Joropo: The national upbeat folk dance and musical style originating from the plains. Dancing Devils of Yare ( Diablos Danzantes de Yare ): A traditional Corpus Christi festival where dancers wear vibrant red costumes and masks to symbolize the triumph of good over evil.

title: Democratic Republic of the Congo Lore
originalText: The dense Congolese rainforest and its vast river systems act as the backdrop for most mythological entities, viewed as conscious, spiritual realms. Biloko : In the mythology of the Mongo people, these are lingering, vengeful spirits of ancestors who roam the deep forests as vicious, dwarf-like entities. They are often characterized by insatiable appetites and serve as a warning against wandering into the jungle unprepared. Minkisi (Singular: Nkisi ): Deeply rooted in Bakongo mythology, these are both supernatural spirits and the charms or objects that house their power. They act as intermediaries to heal the sick, maintain balance, and solve disputes. Nzambi Mpungu: The supreme creator god in many Bantu and Bakongo traditions. He is often distant but occasionally intervenes in worldly affairs. Bokele: A famous hero figure who, in regional mythology, stole the sun from the sky to bring light and warmth to his village. Lukasa Boards: Unique cultural artifacts belonging to the Luba people; these are intricate, beaded wooden boards that act as historical records and tools for oral storytelling. The Tortoise: Frequently depicted as the cleverest animal, using its intelligence and patience to outwit larger predators like leopards and eagles, representing the triumph of brains over brawn. The Spider: Another celebrated trickster figure who frequently embarks on perilous journeys—such as retrieving heavenly fire—to prove his worth or secure a bride. Mokele-mbembe: Perhaps the most famous legend. Indigenous folklore describes this as a massive, amphibious, plant-eating water monster that resides in the swamps of the Congo River basin, often described in terms reminiscent of a sauropod dinosaur. J'ba Fofi: Enormous, spider-like creatures said to build camouflaged webs on the forest floor.

title: England Lore
originalText: East Anglia: Home to Black Shuck—a massive, red-eyed spectral dog that foretells death—and the Green Children, who mysteriously appeared in the 12th century speaking an unknown language. The Midlands: The stomping ground of outlaw Robin Hood , who took from the rich and gave to the poor in Sherwood Forest. The South West : Cornwall and Devon are steeped in magic, featuring tales of mischievous Pixies and ancient legends of King Arthur at Tintagel Castle. The North: Features terrifying water hags like Jenny Greenteeth and the destructive Lambton Worm dragon (County Durham). London & The South East : Protected by the legendary giants Gog and Magog , and haunted by forest spirits like Herne the Hunter in Windsor.

title: Chad Lore
originalText: Chadian folklore blends North African and sub-Saharan traditions, focusing on oral tales from various ethnic groups and the Wodaabe's ceremonial dances. It includes rich, diverse stories that reflect the unique cultural, historical, and mythological landscape of the region. [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5

title: Fiji Lore
originalText: Degei : The supreme creator god of Fiji, often depicted as a giant snake living deep within the Nakauvadra mountain range on the island of Viti Levu . According to legend, he hatched the first humans from eggs and is responsible for seasonal weather and earthquakes. The Afterlife Journey: The folklore includes a complex soul's journey. Degei acts as the judge of the newly dead, who must pass through the caves of Cibaciba or Drakulu to either reach a paradise known as Burotukula or face punishment. Dakuwaqa: Perhaps the most famous figure in Fijian mythology, he was a fierce shape-shifting shark god. He originally terrorized the islands until he was humbled in battle by a giant octopus guarding the island of Kadavu. In exchange for his life, he swore to protect Fijian fishermen at sea, which is why the people of Kadavu do not fear sharks. The Sacred Turtles of Kadavu: The people of Namuana village hold a traditional ritual where they sing chants to call sea turtles up to the surface. The Veli: These are the "little people" of Fijian folklore. They are mischievous, hairy forest-dwelling sprites that live in hollow trees. They are known to possess magical knowledge (like the secret of firewalking) but can be easily angered if travelers destroy their sacred trees or disrupt the forest. Red Prawns of Vatulele : The legend of Vatulele tells of a beautiful chief's daughter who rejected a mainland suitor, ordering him to be thrown from a cliff. As he fell, his gift of cooked prawns transformed into the bright scarlet prawns found in the island's rocky pools today, which locals revere as sacred. The Great Flood & Canoes: In addition to Degei's stories, there are accounts of a great flood and of the god of carpenters teaching the early people how to construct outrigger canoes. Firewalking ( Vilavilairevo ): Originating from the island of Beqa, legend dictates that the Sawau tribe gained the supernatural ability to walk across burning hot stones after a chief struck a deal with a forest spirit ( veli ).

title: Cuban Lore
originalText: Elegguá : The mischievous trickster and gatekeeper of all paths who dances between the living and spirit worlds. Yemayá : The powerful goddess of the sea and mother of all. Changó : The fiercely vibrant Orisha of thunder, lightning, and justice. Resource: Explore Afro-Cuban deities at the Casa de Africa museum in Old Havana. El Güije : A small, shadowy, mischievous goblin-like creature that lives in rivers and ponds. La Madre de Aguas: A giant, mythical snake that guards the island's water sources and rivers. El Cagüeiro : A famous shape-shifting myth from eastern Cuba capable of dangerous transformation. La Luz de Yara: A popular legend of a glowing light seen at night near the town of Yara, originally believed to be the burning flames of the Taíno chief Hatuey. Opia : Gentle spirits of children who passed away too young, thought to live between worlds and symbolized by fireflies. La Llorona / La Gritona : The Cuban variation of the weeping woman haunting rural fields and mountain roads. Martina Kukaracha: A famous Cuban/Spanish folktale of a beautiful Havana cockroach who holds court with various suitors before ultimately marrying a mouse.

title: Singapore Lore
originalText: Sang Nila Utama and Singapura: A 13th-century prince from Palembang who threw his crown into the sea during a storm to save his ship. Landing on Temasek, he spotted a majestic beast he believed was a lion ( singa ), naming the island Singapura ("Lion City"). Redhill (Bukit Merah): The tragic tale of a village plagued by leaping swordfish. A clever boy named Nadim suggested building barricades of banana tree trunks, which trapped the fish by their snouts. Fearing his growing brilliance, the jealous Sultan ordered the boy killed on a hill, staining the soil red. Kusu Island: Legend says a magical giant turtle turned itself into an island to rescue shipwrecked Malay and Chinese sailors, who later built shrines and a temple there. Pulau Ubin and Pulau Sekudu : An elephant, a pig, and a frog challenged each other to swim to Johor. Those who failed were turned to stone; the frog became Frog Island ( Pulau Sekudu ). Badang the Strongman: An ordinary slave who gained superhuman strength after capturing a supernatural forest spirit, becoming a legendary hero of the ancient Singapura kingdom. The Pontianak: Southeast Asia's most famous vampiric female ghost, believed to be the spirit of a woman who died during childbirth, haunting banana trees with a chilling wail and the scent of frangipani. The Midnight Radio Spirit: A common National Service urban legend in military barracks where an unseen entity persistently tunes transistor radios to late-night Chinese broadcasts, regardless of how often it is turned off or unplugged. The Punggol Tiger Spirit: Folklore surrounding northeast Singapore suggesting a mystical white tiger spirit guards the land where old pig farms once stood
